blocks.text:
A synchronous call couples the caller to the availability, latency and capacity of the callee. When an order service calls a payment service, a notification service and an inventory service in sequence, the response time of the order request is the sum of the three, and a failure in any one of them becomes a failure of the order. Asynchronous messaging removes that coupling: the order service records the fact that an order was created and returns, and each interested service consumes the fact at its own pace. The price is a different consistency model (eventual consistency), a new class of failure (duplicates, reordering, lag) and new operational surface (the broker).

This chapter covers the Spring side of that design: `KafkaTemplate`, `@KafkaListener`, serialisation, error handling, retry topics, dead-letter topics, transactions, rebalancing and the outbox pattern. The Kafka concepts themselves (log structure, replication, broker internals) are summarised only to the depth needed to reason about Spring behaviour; a separate Kafka guide covers the broker in depth.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Queue versus log

A classic message queue (RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ) holds messages until a consumer acknowledges them; the broker then deletes the message. Delivery state lives in the broker, routing is flexible (exchanges, bindings), and each message is processed by one consumer of a queue. A log (Kafka) is an append-only, partitioned, replicated sequence of records. The broker never tracks per-message delivery. It retains records for a configured time or size, and each consumer group stores only an offset per partition. Consequences: records can be replayed, any number of independent groups can read the same topic, and the throughput per partition is sequential-disk fast. The cost is that ordering is per partition only, and that individual messages cannot be acknowledged out of order without extra machinery.

blocks.text:
#### Kafka concepts used by Spring

A **topic** is split into **partitions**. Each partition is an ordered log in which every record has an **offset**. A producer chooses the partition: with a non-null key, the default partitioner hashes the key (murmur2) modulo the partition count, so all records of one key land in one partition and keep their relative order. A **consumer group** is a set of consumers sharing a `group.id`; the group coordinator on the broker assigns each partition to exactly one member. Parallelism of a group is therefore bounded by the partition count. The group commits the **offset** of the next record to read, per partition, into the internal topic `__consumer_offsets`. After a restart or a rebalance, consumption resumes at the committed offset.

blocks.text:
#### The Spring layers

Spring Boot auto-configures the following beans when `spring-kafka` is on the classpath and `spring.kafka.*` properties exist: a `KafkaAdmin` (creates `NewTopic` beans at startup), a `ProducerFactory` and `KafkaTemplate`, a `ConsumerFactory` and a `ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory`. The annotation `@KafkaListener` is processed by `KafkaListenerAnnotationBeanPostProcessor`, which registers a `KafkaListenerEndpoint` with the `KafkaListenerEndpointRegistry`. For each endpoint the registry creates a `ConcurrentMessageListenerContainer`, which in turn starts `concurrency` instances of `KafkaMessageListenerContainer`. Each of those owns one `KafkaConsumer` and one thread that runs the poll loop: `poll()`, invoke the listener for each record, commit offsets according to the ack mode, repeat. The listener method therefore runs on the consumer thread, and a slow listener delays the next `poll()`.

#### The producer path

`KafkaTemplate.send()` serialises the key and value, selects a partition, and appends the record to a per-partition batch in the `RecordAccumulator`. A dedicated sender thread ships the batch when it is full (`batch.size`, default 16 KiB) or when `linger.ms` expires (default 0, meaning send as soon as possible). The call returns a `CompletableFuture<SendResult>` (Spring for Apache Kafka 3.0 and later; earlier versions returned `ListenableFuture`). Completion of that future, not return of `send()`, is the moment at which the broker acknowledged the record.

blocks.text:
With `acks=all` the leader replies only after all in-sync replicas have the record; `min.insync.replicas` (for example 2 with replication factor 3) sets the lower bound of replicas that must be in sync for a write to succeed at all. Since Kafka clients 3.0 the defaults are `acks=all` and `enable.idempotence=true`; the idempotent producer attaches a producer id and a per-partition sequence number so that the broker discards duplicates caused by internal retries. Idempotence protects against duplicates inside one producer session only; it does not make an application-level retry (a second `send()` of the same business event) idempotent.

### Hands-on

The mechanism behind ordering, group assignment and duplicate delivery can be demonstrated without a broker. The following plain-JDK program implements a partitioned log, a key-based partitioner, a consumer group with range-style assignment and committed offsets. It then simulates a consumer that processes records and crashes before committing, which is the situation behind every duplicate in Kafka consumers. The program is deterministic because `String.hashCode()` is specified.

blocks.title: MiniLog.java

blocks.code:
$ java MiniLog.java
produced order-1  -> partition 1 offset 0
produced order-2  -> partition 2 offset 0
produced order-3  -> partition 0 offset 0
produced order-0  -> partition 0 offset 1
produced order-1  -> partition 1 offset 1
produced order-2  -> partition 2 offset 1
produced order-3  -> partition 0 offset 2
produced order-0  -> partition 0 offset 3
produced order-1  -> partition 1 offset 2
-- per-key ordering check
partition 0: order-3/event-3, order-0/event-4, order-3/event-7, order-0/event-8
partition 1: order-1/event-1, order-1/event-5, order-1/event-9
partition 2: order-2/event-2, order-2/event-6
rebalance -> {A=[0, 1, 2]}
A polled [event-3, event-4, event-7, event-8]
A committed {0=4, 1=0, 2=0}
rebalance -> {A=[0, 2], B=[1]}
-- A polls 3 more, processes them, crashes BEFORE commit
A processed [event-2, event-6] (not committed)
rebalance -> {B=[0, 1, 2]}
B polled [event-1, event-5, event-9, event-2, event-6]
DUPLICATE delivery: event-2
DUPLICATE delivery: event-6
distinct events delivered: 9 of 9
blocks.title: Output of the in-memory log simulation (run on the build machine)

blocks.text: Three observations follow from the output. First, all records with key `order-1` are in partition 1 in production order (`event-1`, `event-5`, `event-9`), which is the ordering guarantee. Second, the committed offsets after the first poll are `{0=4, 1=0, 2=0}`: only partition 0 was read and committed. Third, consumer A processed `event-2` and `event-6` but crashed before committing; the new owner resumed from committed offset 0 on partition 2 and delivered both again. Nothing was lost, and two records were processed twice. This is **at-least-once** delivery.

The column `LAG` is `LOG-END-OFFSET` minus `CURRENT-OFFSET` (the committed offset). Lag per partition, not the total, shows whether a single partition is stuck.

### Offsets, ack modes and delivery semantics

When the offset is committed relative to the processing defines the delivery guarantee.

- Commit before processing gives **at-most-once**: a crash loses the record.
- Commit after processing gives **at-least-once**: a crash duplicates the record.
- **Exactly-once** across arbitrary side effects does not exist. Kafka provides exactly-once semantics only for the read-process-write cycle inside Kafka (transactions); a side effect such as a database write or an HTTP call is outside that boundary and must be made idempotent.

With `enable.auto.commit=true` the Kafka consumer itself commits the offsets returned by the last `poll()` every `auto.commit.interval.ms` (5 s by default) on the next poll. Those offsets may include records that are still in progress in the listener, and a crash after such a commit loses them. Spring therefore sets auto-commit to false in the container and commits through the `AckMode`:

rows: commit after each record has been processed by the listener
default; commit after all records returned by one poll() were processed
commit after a time or record threshold
listener calls Acknowledgment.acknowledge(); the container commits at the end of the batch
the commit is executed immediately on acknowledge()
blocks.caption: Spring Kafka listener ack modes (ContainerProperties.AckMode).

blocks.text:
`RECORD` costs one commit round trip per record and bounds the replay window after a crash to a single record. `BATCH` is cheaper and replays up to `max.poll.records` records. A rule of thumb for a business service: use `RECORD` or `BATCH`, keep the listener idempotent, and never use broker auto-commit.

### Consumer groups and rebalancing

A rebalance moves partitions between group members. It is triggered by a member joining or leaving, a missed heartbeat (`session.timeout.ms`, default 45 s in Kafka 3.0 and later), a poll loop that does not call `poll()` within `max.poll.interval.ms` (default 5 minutes), or a change in the partition count. During an eager rebalance (the behaviour of `RangeAssignor` and `RoundRobinAssignor`) every member revokes all partitions and processing stops group-wide. The `CooperativeStickyAssignor` moves only the partitions that must move; Kafka clients since 3.0 list `RangeAssignor` followed by `CooperativeStickyAssignor` as the default, which still allows an eager protocol in practice until `RangeAssignor` is removed from the list. Setting `partition.assignment.strategy` to `org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.CooperativeStickyAssignor` once all members are upgraded gives incremental rebalancing. Kafka 4.0 additionally introduces a broker-driven consumer group protocol (KIP-848, enabled client-side by `group.protocol=consumer`) that removes the group-wide synchronisation barrier; its adoption in Spring Boot applications should be checked against the Spring for Apache Kafka version in use.

Two settings reduce unnecessary rebalances in Kubernetes, where pods restart often: **static membership** (`group.instance.id` set to the stable pod name of a StatefulSet; a restart within `session.timeout.ms` does not trigger a rebalance) and a `max.poll.interval.ms` that exceeds the worst-case processing time of one `poll()` batch.

Spring exposes rebalance events through `ConsumerAwareRebalanceListener` and publishes `ConsumerStartedEvent`, `ListenerContainerIdleEvent` and similar application events. Offsets for in-flight records should be committed in `onPartitionsRevoked` when `MANUAL` acknowledgement is used.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How many consumers should a group have, and what happens if there are more consumers than partitions? At most one consumer per partition receives data. With six partitions, a group of eight consumers has two idle members. The partition count is therefore the upper bound of parallelism, and it must be chosen with expected peak throughput in mind because increasing it later changes the key-to-partition mapping and breaks per-key ordering across the change.

### Error handling, retry topics and dead-letter topics

The container invokes the listener inside a try block and passes any exception to a `CommonErrorHandler`. Since Spring for Apache Kafka 2.8 the default is `DefaultErrorHandler`, which replaces the older `SeekToCurrentErrorHandler`. On failure it **seeks** the consumer back to the failed record (so the failed record and all unprocessed records of the poll are redelivered by the next `poll()`), waits according to its `BackOff`, and after the back-off is exhausted calls a **recoverer**. The default back-off is `FixedBackOff(0L, 9)`: no delay and nine retries, that is ten delivery attempts in total, after which the record is logged at ERROR level and skipped. Because the retries run on the consumer thread with the partition blocked, a long back-off delays every record behind the failing one and counts towards `max.poll.interval.ms`.

Some exceptions are classified as not retryable and go straight to the recoverer: `DeserializationException`, `MessageConversionException`, `ConversionException`, `MethodArgumentResolutionException`, `NoSuchMethodException` and `ClassCastException`. Further types are added with `addNotRetryableExceptions(...)`. Only `RuntimeException` subclasses are handled; an `Error` terminates the consumer thread.

The recommended recoverer is `DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer`, which publishes the failed record to `<topic>-dlt` on the same partition number, with headers that carry the exception class, message, stack trace and the original topic, partition and offset. The dead-letter topic therefore needs at least as many partitions as the source topic unless a custom destination resolver is supplied.

blocks.title: KafkaConsumerConfig.java

blocks.text:
Spring Boot detects a single `CommonErrorHandler` bean and applies it to the auto-configured `ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory`; no explicit factory is needed. `ExponentialBackOff.setMaxAttempts` is available from Spring Framework 6.1; earlier versions bound the sequence with `setMaxElapsedTime`.

#### Non-blocking retries with @RetryableTopic

Blocking retries preserve order but stall the partition. For failures that are transient and independent per record (a downstream outage of two minutes), **retry topics** move the failing record away from the main topic and continue with the next record. Spring creates a chain of topics; the consumer of each retry topic pauses the partition until the due time stored in a header has passed.

blocks.title: PaymentRequestListener.java

blocks.text: With four attempts and exponential back-off, the framework creates `orders.events-retry-1000`, `orders.events-retry-2000`, `orders.events-retry-4000` and `orders.events-dlt`. The annotation class `@Backoff` is the one from `org.springframework.retry.annotation`, so `spring-retry` must be on the classpath. The name of the exception class `PaymentGatewayUnavailableException` stands for any application exception marking a transient failure.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Retry topics break per-key ordering. A second event for the same order may be processed while the first waits in a retry topic. Domain logic must then tolerate out-of-order arrival, for example by rejecting transitions that are illegal in the current state of the aggregate or by comparing a version number carried in the event.

#### Poison messages and the dead-letter topic

A **poison message** is a record that fails deterministically (a malformed payload, a violated business rule). Without a dead-letter path and a bounded retry count, the partition makes no progress; consumer lag on exactly one partition grows without bound. A dead-letter topic is useful only if it is monitored (an alert on records per minute), if records can be replayed after the cause is fixed (a small admin endpoint or a script that republishes from `-dlt` to the source topic), and if the headers allow root-cause analysis.

### Producer reliability, idempotence and transactions

The producer settings that decide durability are `acks`, `enable.idempotence`, `retries` and `delivery.timeout.ms` (default 120 s, an upper bound on the total time including retries). With the defaults of Kafka clients 3.0 and later (`acks=all`, idempotence on, `retries=Integer.MAX_VALUE` bounded by the delivery timeout) a record is neither lost nor duplicated by transient network errors within one producer session. Order within a partition is retained for up to five in-flight requests when idempotence is enabled.

**Kafka transactions** let a producer write to several partitions atomically and, combined with `sendOffsetsToTransaction`, commit consumer offsets in the same transaction. This yields exactly-once for the consume-transform-produce pattern between topics. Spring enables it with a transaction id prefix; the `KafkaTransactionManager` or the container participates.

blocks.code:
spring:
  kafka:
    producer:
      transaction-id-prefix: tx-enrich-
    consumer:
      isolation-level: read_committed
      enable-auto-commit: false
blocks.title: application.yml (transactional processor)

blocks.text:
When `transaction-id-prefix` is set, Boot creates a `KafkaTransactionManager`, and the listener container starts a Kafka transaction for each record or batch; offsets and the records the listener sends via `KafkaTemplate` commit or abort together. Downstream consumers must use `isolation.level=read_committed` or they also read records of aborted transactions.

Limits that interview answers should state explicitly. Exactly-once applies only while all reads and writes are in Kafka; a database update or an e-mail sent inside the listener is not part of the transaction and repeats if the transaction aborts and the record is redelivered. Mixing a JPA transaction and a Kafka transaction gives at best best-effort one-phase commit (`ChainedTransactionManager` is deprecated and removed in recent releases); the supported answer for database plus Kafka is the outbox pattern, not a distributed transaction.

### The outbox pattern with Kafka

The dual-write problem: a service must update its database and publish an event, and no transaction spans both. If the service commits and then crashes before `send()`, the event is lost; if it sends first and the commit fails, the event describes a state that never existed. The transactional outbox writes the event into an `outbox` table in the same database transaction as the business change. A separate relay reads unsent rows and publishes them to Kafka, then marks them as sent.

blocks.text: The following plain-JDK program contrasts a dual write with an outbox. The in-memory `Db` rolls back all tables when a transaction body throws; crashes are injected after the commit, and a relay crash is injected after publishing but before marking the row as sent.

blocks.title: Outbox.java

blocks.code:
$ java Outbox.java
  !! process killed
dual write   -> orders=[o-1] broker=[]
  !! process killed
outbox write -> orders=[o-1] outbox rows=1 broker=[]
  !! relay died
relay restarted -> broker=[OrderCreated:o-1, OrderCreated:o-1]
blocks.title: Output of the outbox simulation (run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
The dual write ends with the order in the database and nothing on the broker: a lost event. With the outbox, the order and the pending event survive the crash; after the relay restarts the event is published, and because the relay died before marking the row, it is published twice. The consumer must therefore deduplicate on the event identifier.

The Spring implementation uses a JPA entity, a repository with a locking query for multi-instance relays, and a scheduled relay.

OutboxRepository.java

blocks.text: `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` lets several relay instances poll the same table without blocking each other and without publishing the same row concurrently; each row is locked by exactly one transaction. Named parameters in native queries require `-parameters` compilation, which the Spring Boot Maven plugin parent enables.

blocks.title: OutboxRelay.java

blocks.text:
What to notice: the relay waits for the broker acknowledgement before marking the row, so success of `get()` implies durability on the broker; a failure rolls back the transaction and the rows stay pending; and the `String` template means the payload is already JSON, so the relay needs no knowledge of event classes. Production relays often replace polling with change data capture (Debezium reading the write-ahead log), which removes the polling delay and the load on the table.

The producer in the service layer writes the business row and the outbox row inside one `@Transactional` method:

#### The idempotent consumer

A consumer is idempotent when processing the same event twice has the same effect as processing it once. The standard implementation stores processed event identifiers in a table with a unique constraint, inside the same database transaction as the business effect.

blocks.title: PaymentService.java
Watch out
blocks.text: The catch block above is only safe if the exception does not poison the transaction. With some JPA providers and databases, a unique violation marks the transaction rollback-only or aborts the PostgreSQL transaction (SQLSTATE 25P02). The robust variant uses `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` through a native query and inspects the affected row count; zero affected rows means duplicate.

### Schema evolution and the event contract

An event in a topic outlives the code that produced it, and consumers deploy independently. The rules for compatible evolution are the same as for REST payloads, with the difference that old events remain in the log.

- Adding an optional field is compatible in both directions when consumers ignore unknown properties (`spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-unknown-properties=false`, the Boot default).
- Removing or renaming a field, or changing its type, is breaking. The two-step procedure is: add the new field and publish both; migrate all consumers; stop publishing the old field.
- A schema registry (Confluent Schema Registry, Apicurio) with Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema enforces a compatibility mode (BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL) at publish time and stores the schema id inside the record, which removes the need for type headers.
- Include a `type` and a `version` in the payload or headers so that one topic can carry several event kinds and a consumer can route on them.
- Never reuse a topic for a different meaning; create `orders.events.v2` and run both until consumers have migrated.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: consumer lag keeps growing

**Scenario.** The `payment-service` consumes `orders.events` with three instances. After a marketing campaign the lag on partitions 2 and 4 grows steadily while partitions 0, 1, 3 and 5 stay at zero. **Symptoms.** Alerts on `records-lag-max`; payments delayed by minutes; no errors in the logs. **Diagnosis.** Run `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group` `payment-service` and read `LAG` per partition. Skewed lag on two partitions points to hot keys or a slow instance, not to total capacity. Take a thread dump of the instance that owns those partitions with `jcmd <pid> Thread.print`; the consumer threads (`org.springframework.kafka.KafkaListenerEndpointContainer#0-2-C-1`) show the blocking call. Check the Actuator metric `kafka.consumer.fetch.manager.records.lag.max` and the listener timer `spring.kafka.listener`. **Root cause.** The listener performed a synchronous HTTP call to the payment gateway without a timeout; two keys with large order volumes (a corporate customer) hash to partitions 2 and 4, and each call took four seconds under load. **Fix.** Set connect and read timeouts on the client, move the call behind a circuit breaker with a bulkhead, raise `concurrency` to the partition count, and if one key is genuinely hot, key by `orderId` instead of `customerId`. **Prevention.** Alert on per-partition lag growth rate rather than a fixed threshold, load-test with a skewed key distribution, and require timeouts on every outbound call in code review.

blocks.text:
#### Problem 2: a poison message blocks one partition

**Scenario.** A producer bug publishes one record with a null `total`. The consumer throws `NullPointerException` on it. **Symptoms.** Lag on a single partition grows without bound; the same stack trace repeats in the log every few seconds; other partitions are healthy. **Diagnosis.** Grep the log for the repeated offset (`partition=3 offset=88123`); inspect the record with `kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic orders.events --partition 3 --offset 88123 --max-messages`

1. `1`. **Root cause.** A custom error handler with `FixedBackOff.UNLIMITED_ATTEMPTS` retried the record forever, and no

dead-letter topic existed. **Fix.** Use `DefaultErrorHandler` with a bounded `BackOff` and a `DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer`; register deterministic exceptions as not retryable; validate the payload on the producer side. **Prevention.** Alert on dead-letter topic traffic, test a malformed record in an integration test with Testcontainers, and keep unbounded retries out of listeners.

#### Problem 3: duplicate processing after a rebalance

**Scenario.** During a rolling update the payment service charged some customers twice. **Symptoms.** Two `Payment` rows for one `orderId`; the logs show the same offset processed by two different pods within a minute. **Diagnosis.** Compare `partition` and `offset` in both log lines; check the logs for `Revoking previously assigned partitions` and `Rebalance` entries between them; look at `max.poll.interval.ms` versus the processing time of one batch. **Root cause.** The listener was at-least-once by design, but the write was not idempotent. A pod was terminated after charging and before the offset commit, and the new owner replayed the record. **Fix.** The idempotent consumer shown earlier: a unique `event_id` constraint written in the same transaction, plus a unique index on `payment(order_id)`. **Prevention.** Treat duplicates as normal. Use `RECORD` ack mode and graceful shutdown to shrink the window, but rely on idempotence for correctness.

#### Problem 4: message loss with auto-commit

**Scenario.** After an out-of-memory crash of a consumer, about 300 events never appear in the downstream database, although the consumer group shows zero lag. **Symptoms.** Missing rows with no error trace; offsets are ahead of the data. **Diagnosis.** Compare the committed offset of the group with the highest offset successfully written to the database. Inspect the effective configuration with `--debug` logging of `ConsumerConfig values` at startup: `enable.auto.commit = true`. **Root cause.** The property `spring.kafka.consumer.enable-auto-commit=true` had been copied from a tutorial; the Kafka client committed the offsets of the polled batch every five seconds while the listener handed the records to an in-memory executor that had not yet finished. **Fix.** Set `enable-auto-commit: false`, process on the consumer thread or acknowledge manually after the asynchronous work completes, and size `max.poll.records` to the processing capacity. **Prevention.** Keep the Kafka consumer defaults of the container, and review any configuration that hands records to another thread.

### Questions to expect

1. **What does a Kafka consumer group guarantee about partition ownership?** Within one group each partition is assigned to exactly one member at a time. Different groups are independent and each reads all records.
2. **How is ordering guaranteed?** Only within a partition. A key maps to one partition by hashing, so records with the same key are consumed in the order they were written, provided the partition count does not change.
3. **Why can the same message be delivered twice?** The offset commit is separate from the processing. A crash, rebalance or timeout between them replays the uncommitted records. Idempotent consumers absorb this.
4. **What does** `acks=all` **do, and what is** `min.insync.replicas` **for?** The leader acknowledges after all in-sync replicas have the record. `min.insync.replicas` sets the least number of in-sync replicas that must exist for the write to be accepted; with replication factor 3 and a minimum of 2, one broker may fail without data loss or unavailability of writes.
5. **What is the difference between blocking retries and retry topics?** Blocking retries re-run the record on the consumer thread and keep order but stall the partition. Retry topics publish the record to delayed topics and continue; order is lost.
6. **What is a dead-letter topic?** A topic that receives records that exhausted their retries or are not retryable, with the failure reason in headers, so that the main flow continues and the records can be analysed and replayed.
7. **Explain exactly-once in Kafka.** Idempotent producers plus transactions give atomic read-process-write between Kafka topics. External side effects are outside the guarantee and need idempotence or the outbox pattern.
8. **What is the outbox pattern and why is it needed?** It writes the event into a table in the same database transaction as the state change and publishes it asynchronously, which avoids the lost update or phantom event of a dual write. Delivery is at-least-once.
9. **What triggers a consumer group rebalance?** Members joining or leaving, missed heartbeats, exceeding `max.poll.interval.ms`, and partition count changes. Cooperative assignors and static membership reduce the disruption.
10. **How is a poison message handled?** Classify the exception as not retryable or bound the retries, send the record to the dead-letter topic, alert, fix the cause and replay.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Kafka guarantees order only within a partition, so the record key is a design decision tied to the aggregate that needs ordering.

- Offsets commit after processing gives at-least-once; every consumer must be idempotent, typically with a unique event id in the same transaction as the effect.
- `DefaultErrorHandler` with a bounded back-off and a `DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer` prevents poison messages from blocking a partition; `@RetryableTopic` trades ordering for availability.
- Exactly-once holds only inside Kafka; database plus Kafka consistency is achieved with the transactional outbox.
- Lag per partition, rebalance frequency and dead-letter traffic are the three operational signals to monitor.

sections.title: RabbitMQ, Scheduling, Async Work and Events

blocks.text:
Kafka is one answer to asynchronous work and not always the most appropriate. Task distribution with flexible routing, per-message acknowledgement and delayed redelivery is the strength of an AMQP broker such as RabbitMQ. Work that stays inside one JVM needs no broker at all: `@Async`, `@Scheduled` and Spring application events cover it. This chapter explains each mechanism, the thread and failure model behind it, and the criteria for choosing between them.

### Concept and mechanism

#### RabbitMQ and Spring AMQP

In AMQP 0-9-1 a producer publishes to an **exchange**, never directly to a queue. The exchange routes the message to zero or more **queues** according to **bindings**; consumers read from queues. Exchange types: `direct` (exact routing key match), `topic` (pattern match with `*` for one word and `#` for zero or more words), `fanout` (all bound queues) and `headers`. A message is removed from a queue when the consumer acknowledges it. A message that is rejected without requeue, expires (TTL) or overflows a queue length limit is republished to the queue's **dead-letter exchange** (DLX).

blocks.text:
Spring AMQP provides `RabbitTemplate` for publishing, `@RabbitListener` for consuming (executed by a `SimpleMessageListenerContainer` or `DirectMessageListenerContainer`), and `RabbitAdmin`, which declares exchanges, queues and bindings from `@Bean` definitions at connection time. Boot auto-configures `CachingConnectionFactory`, `RabbitTemplate`, `RabbitAdmin` and the listener container factory from `spring.rabbitmq.*`.

The default acknowledge mode of the Spring listener container is `AUTO`: the container acknowledges when the listener returns normally and rejects when it throws. The default for a rejected message is to **requeue** it (`spring.rabbitmq.listener.simple.default-requeue-rejected=true`), which for a deterministic failure produces an endless hot loop. Setting it to `false`, or throwing `AmqpRejectAndDontRequeueException`, sends the message to the DLX.

#### Scheduling

`@Scheduled` methods run on a `TaskScheduler`. Boot auto-configures a `ThreadPoolTaskScheduler` with a pool size of one (`spring.task.scheduling.pool.size=1`), so two long-running scheduled methods delay each other. `fixedRate` starts runs at fixed intervals measured start to start (overlapping runs are not started by the single-threaded scheduler; the next run starts late), `fixedDelay` waits the given time after the previous run finished, and `cron` follows a calendar expression with six fields in Spring (seconds first). Scheduling runs in every instance of the application; with three replicas, a nightly job executes three times unless coordinated. The options are a distributed lock (ShedLock, which uses a row in a shared table or a Redis key), a leader election, or a clustered scheduler such as Quartz with a JDBC job store, in which triggers are persisted and claimed by exactly one node.

#### Asynchronous execution with @Async

`@Async` is implemented by `AsyncAnnotationBeanPostProcessor`, which wraps the bean in an AOP proxy whose `AsyncExecutionInterceptor` submits the invocation to a `TaskExecutor` and returns immediately. It is therefore subject to the same limits as every proxy-based feature: self-invocation and `private` or `final` methods bypass it. Boot auto-configures `applicationTaskExecutor` (a `ThreadPoolTaskExecutor` with core size 8, an unbounded queue and an effectively unbounded maximum size, which means only eight threads ever run because the queue never fills). With `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` (Spring Boot 3.2 and later, JDK 21) the executor is a `SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor` that starts a virtual thread per task. Neither the `SecurityContext` nor the SLF4J MDC is propagated to the executor thread by default; a `TaskDecorator` copies them.

#### Application events

`ApplicationEventPublisher.publishEvent()` calls every matching `@EventListener` synchronously on the publishing thread, by default inside the publisher's transaction. Methods annotated `@TransactionalEventListener` (phase `AFTER_COMMIT` by default) are deferred by `TransactionSynchronization` until the transaction completes; they are skipped if the transaction rolls back, and if no transaction is active the event is dropped unless `fallbackExecution =` `true`.

### Worked example

The `billing` and `email` queues of the example diagram, declared as beans, with a dead-letter exchange and JSON conversion.

blocks.title: RabbitConfig.java

blocks.text: Boot detects a `MessageConverter` bean and applies it to the `RabbitTemplate` and to the listener container factory. Without it, the template serialises payloads with Java serialisation, which is both insecure and unreadable for other consumers.

blocks.title: BillingListener.java

blocks.code:
spring:
  rabbitmq:
    host: localhost
    port: 5672
    username: ${RABBIT_USER}
    password: ${RABBIT_PASSWORD}
    publisher-confirm-type: correlated
    publisher-returns: true
    listener:
      simple:
        acknowledge-mode: auto
        default-requeue-rejected: false
        prefetch: 20
        concurrency: 2
        max-concurrency: 8
        retry:
          enabled: true
          max-attempts: 3
          initial-interval: 1s
          multiplier: 2
blocks.title: application.yml (fragment)

blocks.text:
`publisher-confirm-type: correlated` makes the broker confirm each publish; without confirms, a publish can be lost silently when the broker crashes. `publisher-returns` reports messages that matched no queue (mandatory flag). The `retry` block configures stateless in-memory retries inside the container; after the attempts are exhausted the message is rejected without requeue and reaches the DLX.

Scheduling and asynchronous work with explicit executors:

blocks.title: AsyncConfig.java
MailService.java

blocks.text:
The executor is bounded and uses `CallerRunsPolicy`: when eight threads are busy and 200 tasks queue up, the submitting thread executes the task itself, which slows the producer down instead of growing memory. An exception thrown from a `void @Async` method is not visible to the caller; it goes to the `AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler` (a logging handler by default), so a method that returns `CompletableFuture` is preferable.

A transactional event listener that keeps a cache consistent without coupling the service to the cache:

blocks.title: ProductEvents.java

blocks.text:
The service calls `publisher.publishEvent(new ProductChanged(id))` inside its `@Transactional` method. The eviction runs only after a successful commit, which removes the window in which a concurrent reader repopulates the cache from the not yet committed old row.

### Hands-on

Run RabbitMQ locally and observe routing:

blocks.code:
$ docker run -d --name rabbit -p 5672:5672 -p 15672:15672 rabbitmq:3-management
$ ./mvnw spring-boot:run
$ curl -X POST localhost:8080/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"customerId":"c-1","total":12.50}'
$ docker exec rabbit rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages consumers
Timeout: 60.0 seconds ...
Listing queues for vhost / ...
name        messages  consumers
billing.q   0         2
billing.dlq 0         0
blocks.title: typical output (not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
A malformed message published from the management UI (`total` missing) moves to `billing.dlq` after the three configured attempts, and `rabbitmqctl list_queues` then shows `billing.dlq 1 0`. The headers `x-death` and `x-first-death-reason` on that message name the queue and the reason (`rejected`).

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: a scheduled job runs three times

**Scenario.** The reporting job `@Scheduled(cron = "0 0 2 * * *")` sends a daily summary mail. After scaling to three replicas, every recipient gets three mails. **Symptoms.** Identical log lines at 02:00:00 from three pods; duplicated side effects. **Diagnosis.** `kubectl logs` of each pod filtered by the job's logger shows concurrent execution; the scheduler is local to each JVM. **Root cause.** `@Scheduled` has no cluster awareness. **Fix.** Guard the method with ShedLock (`@SchedulerLock(name = "dailySummary", lockAtMostFor = "10m", lockAtLeastFor = "1m")` with a JDBC or Redis lock provider), or move the job to a Kubernetes `CronJob` that runs one pod, or use Quartz with `spring.quartz.job-store-type=jdbc` and `org.quartz.jobStore.isClustered=true`. **Prevention.** Treat every scheduled method as a distributed-systems concern; also make the job idempotent (a `summary_sent` flag per day) so that an overlapping run is harmless.

#### Problem 2: @Async silently runs synchronously

**Scenario.** `OrderService.place()` calls `this.sendConfirmation(...)`, annotated `@Async`, and the HTTP response still takes two seconds. **Symptoms.** The log line of the mail method shows the `http-nio-8080-exec-3` thread instead of `mail-1`. **Diagnosis.** Log `Thread.currentThread().getName()` in the async method; inspect the bean class with `AopUtils.isAopProxy(bean)`. **Root cause.** Self-invocation: the call goes through `this`, not through the proxy, so `AsyncExecutionInterceptor` never runs. Also verify that `@EnableAsync` is present; without it the annotation is ignored. **Fix.** Move the method into a separate bean and inject it, or inject the proxy of the class itself with `@Lazy`. **Prevention.** Keep proxy-based annotations at the boundary between beans; the chapter on AOP and proxies in the first part of this guide describes the mechanism.

#### Problem 3: RabbitMQ message redelivered in an endless loop

**Scenario.** A listener throws `IllegalStateException` for a particular message; the CPU of the consumer is at 100 per cent and the broker shows the message with `redelivered: true` thousands of times per minute. **Symptoms.** Log flooding with the same stack trace; queue depth does not drop. **Diagnosis.** In the management UI, the queue shows an `unacked` count of 1 and a high deliver rate with a zero ack rate. **Root cause.** The default `default-requeue-rejected=true` requeues a failed message at the head of the queue. **Fix.** Set `spring.rabbitmq.listener.simple.default-requeue-rejected=false`, enable bounded retry, and configure a DLX on the queue. **Prevention.** Declare a dead-letter exchange for every queue as part of the topology and alert on the dead-letter queue depth.

### Questions to expect

1. **When RabbitMQ and when Kafka?** RabbitMQ for task queues, routing flexibility, priorities and per-message acknowledgement with moderate volume; Kafka for high-throughput event streams, replay and multiple independent consumer groups.
2. **What are the AMQP exchange types?** `direct`, `topic`, `fanout` and `headers`. Producers publish to exchanges; bindings connect exchanges to queues.
3. **What does** `@Async` **need in order to work?** `@EnableAsync`, a call through the Spring proxy (not `this`), a non-final public method, and ideally a configured bounded executor.
4. **Why does** `@Scheduled` **run more than once in a cluster?** Each instance has its own scheduler. A distributed lock, a leader election or a clustered Quartz job store is required for single execution.
5. **What is the difference between** `@EventListener` **and** `@TransactionalEventListener`**?** The first runs synchronously at publication, inside the transaction; the second runs in a transaction phase, by default after commit, and is skipped on rollback.
6. **Why are unbounded executor queues dangerous?** The pool never grows beyond the core size and a backlog accumulates in memory until an `OutOfMemoryError`. A bounded queue with a rejection policy applies back-pressure.
7. **How is the MDC propagated into** `@Async` **threads?** With a `TaskDecorator` that copies `MDC.getCopyOfContextMap()` to the worker thread; the `SecurityContext` needs `DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor` or the equivalent.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
RabbitMQ routes through exchanges and bindings; a dead-letter exchange and `default-requeue-rejected=false` prevent endless redelivery.

- `@Scheduled` and `@Async` are local to one JVM; clustered execution needs ShedLock, Quartz JDBC or a Kubernetes CronJob.
- `@Async`, like every proxy-based annotation, is bypassed by self-invocation; executors must be bounded and decorated to carry the MDC.
- Application events are in-process and non-durable; `@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)` ties side effects to a successful commit.

A cache trades consistency for latency and load. A product page that is read a thousand times for each update does not need a database query per read; a cache in front of the database returns the previous answer in microseconds and removes load from the connection pool. The costs are staleness, a second system to operate, and a set of failure modes (stampede, penetration, inconsistency) that only appear under load. The Redis data structures and persistence model are covered in a separate Redis guide; this chapter covers the Spring Cache abstraction, its Redis integration and the failure modes.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The Spring Cache abstraction

`@EnableCaching` (applied automatically by Boot when a cache starter is present) registers a `BeanFactoryCacheOperationSourceAdvisor`. The advisor wraps beans that have caching annotations in a proxy whose `CacheInterceptor` reads the annotation metadata through `AnnotationCacheOperationSource`, computes a key with a `KeyGenerator` or the SpEL `key` expression, and calls the `Cache` obtained from the `CacheManager`. The business method is a black box: on a hit it is not executed. As with `@Transactional`, the interceptor sits in the proxy, so self-invocation and private methods bypass the cache.

rows: return the cached value if the key exists; otherwise invoke the method and store the result
always invoke the method and store the result (refresh without reading)
remove one key, or all keys with allEntries = true; beforeInvocation = true evicts even if the method throws
combine several operations on one method
class-level defaults such as the cache names
blocks.caption: Cache annotations.

blocks.text:
The default key generator (`SimpleKeyGenerator`) builds the key from all method parameters: no parameter gives `SimpleKey.EMPTY`, one parameter uses the value itself. Explicit keys with SpEL (`key = "#id"`, `key =` `"#root.methodName + #a0"`) are clearer and avoid collisions between methods that share a cache name.

#### Cache-aside with Redis

With `spring.cache.type=redis` Boot creates a `RedisCacheManager` over the `RedisConnectionFactory`. Each cache name is a key prefix in Redis; an entry for cache `products` and key `42` is stored under the Redis key `products::42`. Values are serialised with the configured `RedisSerializer` (JDK serialisation by default, which requires `Serializable` and is unreadable in `redis-cli`; JSON is preferred). Every entry should have a TTL; without one, entries live until evicted by memory policy.

blocks.text: The prefix `spring.data.redis.*` applies to Spring Boot 3.0 and later (it was `spring.redis.*` in 2.x). The timeout of 500 ms bounds how long a request waits for Redis; an unreachable cache must not become an outage of the service.

blocks.title: CacheConfig.java
ProductService.java

blocks.text:
What to notice: `sync = true` makes concurrent callers for the same key in one JVM wait for a single load instead of all executing the method (`RedisCache` serialises the loader per instance; it does not coordinate between application instances); the return type `Product` must be serialisable to JSON and deserialisable without type information problems, which is why entities should not be cached directly (use a DTO or record); and the eviction is event-driven and happens after commit, so a concurrent reader cannot re-cache the pre-update row.

A record is the safest cached value:

blocks.title: ProductView.java

blocks.text:
### Key design, TTL and consistency

**Keys.** A key should identify the value and nothing else: include the entity identifier and, where the value depends on them, the tenant, the locale or a representation version (`products::v2::42`). A change of the cached class layout requires a new prefix or a cache flush, otherwise deserialisation of old entries fails. Parameters that are objects need a stable `toString`/`hashCode` or an explicit SpEL key.

**TTL.** The TTL is the upper bound on staleness, and it protects against missed evictions. Entries that expire at the same moment cause synchronised misses; adding random jitter to TTLs (for example 30 minutes plus or minus 10 per cent) spreads the reload load.

**Consistency with the database.** Cache-aside gives eventual consistency. Two races matter:

- A reader loads the old row, a writer updates the row and evicts, then the reader stores its old value. The cached value is now stale until the TTL expires. Evicting after commit and using short TTLs narrows the window; versioned values (`version` field compared on write, or Redis `SET` with a check script) close it.
- Evicting before the commit lets a concurrent reader re-populate the cache from the old row. For this reason the eviction in the example above is bound to `AFTER_COMMIT`.

**Failure of Redis.** By default a Redis exception propagates from the `CacheInterceptor` and fails the request. A `CacheErrorHandler` bean (via `CachingConfigurer`) can log and continue, which turns a cache outage into a slower service instead of an unavailable one.

### Stampede, penetration and avalanche

A **stampede** (thundering herd, dog-pile) occurs when a hot key expires and many concurrent requests miss at once; every one of them executes the loader against the database. **Penetration** is repeated lookups for keys that do not exist (nothing is ever cached, each request reaches the database). An **avalanche** is the simultaneous expiry of many keys or the loss of the whole cache. The mitigation for a stampede is single flight: one request loads while the others wait or serve the stale value.

The following plain-JDK program fires 200 virtual-thread clients at a cold key with a 200 ms loader, first without protection and then with a lock and a second cache check (double-checked loading), which is what `@Cacheable(sync =` `true)` does within one JVM.

no protection (cold key)           clients=200  db calls=200
single flight (lock + re-check)    clients=200  db calls=1

Mitigations in order of preference: single flight (`sync = true`, or a distributed lock with a short lease for multi-instance protection), TTL jitter, serving stale data while one request refreshes (soft TTL), pre-warming hot keys after a deployment, and caching negative results for a short time (a few seconds) against penetration.

### Hands-on

{"id":42,"name":"Keyboard","price":49.90,"version":3}
$ docker exec redis redis-cli KEYS 'catalog:*'

blocks.text:
The sequence shows the key naming, the TTL counting down from the configured 30 minutes, and the key disappearing after the committed update.

Actuator exposes cache statistics through the metric `cache.gets` with tags `result=hit|miss` and `cache=products` for caches that report statistics; for Redis caches enable them with `spring.cache.redis.enable-statistics=true`. The hit ratio is `hit / (hit + miss)`.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: cache stampede after expiry

**Scenario.** A product list endpoint caches a heavy aggregate query with a TTL of five minutes. Every five minutes the 95th percentile latency spikes from 20 ms to 4 seconds. **Symptoms.** Periodic latency spikes; `hikaricp.connections.pending` rises at the same moments; PostgreSQL shows many identical queries in `pg_stat_activity`. **Diagnosis.** Correlate the spike timestamps with the TTL; run `SELECT query, count(*) FROM` `pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active' GROUP BY query` during a spike and observe the same statement dozens of times. **Root cause.** The key expires, 150 concurrent requests miss, and each runs the 3-second aggregate query. **Fix.** `@Cacheable(sync = true)` for single flight per instance; TTL jitter; for several instances, a Redis lock (`SET key` `value NX PX 5000`) around the loader, or a background refresh job that rewrites the entry before it expires. **Prevention.** Load tests that start from a cold cache, and a dashboard for hit ratio and loader concurrency.

#### Problem 2: stale data after an update

**Scenario.** After a price change the website shows the old price for up to 30 minutes, and occasionally the old price reappears after the new one was visible. **Symptoms.** Support tickets; the database has the new value, `redis-cli GET` returns the old one. **Diagnosis.** Compare the DB row and the cached value; check whether `@CacheEvict` is on a method reached through self-invocation; inspect the order of eviction and commit (log both with timestamps). **Root** **cause.** Two defects: the update method called `evict` through `this` (no proxy), and a second code path (a batch import using JDBC directly) changed the table without touching the cache. The re-appearance came from a reader that had loaded the old row before the commit and stored it after the eviction. **Fix.** Evict through a published event with `AFTER_COMMIT`; route every write path through the service; shorten the TTL of volatile data; store a version in the value and reject writes of an older version. **Prevention.** Define the invariant ("a price is at most 60 seconds stale") per cache, and test the write path with an integration test against a real Redis (Testcontainers).

#### Problem 3: the cache makes things worse when Redis is slow

**Scenario.** A Redis failover takes 20 seconds. During that time all requests of the service time out. **Symptoms.** Tomcat threads blocked in `LettuceConnection`; 5xx rate rises; the database is idle. **Diagnosis.** `jcmd <pid> Thread.print` shows threads waiting in `io.lettuce.core.protocol.AsyncCommand`; the command timeout was the default one minute. **Root cause.** No bounded timeout, and the cache error propagated to the caller. **Fix.** `spring.data.redis.timeout=300ms`, a `CacheErrorHandler` that logs and falls through to the database, and a circuit breaker around cache access for sustained outages. **Prevention.** Treat the cache as optional in every code path, and rehearse its failure.

### Questions to expect

1. **How does** `@Cacheable` **work internally?** A proxy with `CacheInterceptor` checks the `Cache` for the computed key before invoking the method and stores the result on a miss. It is bypassed by self-invocation.
2. **What is the difference between** `@CachePut` **and** `@Cacheable`**?** `@CachePut` always executes the method and updates the cache; `@Cacheable` skips the method on a hit.
3. **What is cache-aside, and what are its alternatives?** The application reads the cache first and loads and stores on a miss. Read-through puts that logic in the cache layer; write-through and write-behind write to the cache and the store together or asynchronously.
4. **What is a cache stampede and how is it prevented?** Many concurrent misses of one key all hit the backend. Single flight (`sync = true` or a lock), TTL jitter and background refresh prevent it.
5. **How can the cache and the database become inconsistent?** A missed or early eviction, a write path that bypasses the cache, and the read-old, write-new, store-old race. Evict after commit, use TTLs and version values.
6. **Why should entities not be cached directly?** They carry lazy proxies and a persistence context association; serialisation fails or triggers lazy loading, and the class layout becomes the cache schema. DTOs or records are stable and small.
7. **What is cache penetration?** Repeated requests for non-existent keys bypass the cache. Cache a negative marker for a short time or use a Bloom filter in front.
8. **What happens when Redis is down?** Without a `CacheErrorHandler`, cache exceptions fail the request. Bounded timeouts and an error handler degrade to database reads.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
`@Cacheable` is a proxy-based, key-driven cache-aside; the key, the TTL and the serialisation format are design decisions, not defaults.

- Evict after commit (`@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)`) and keep a TTL as the safety net.
- A cold hot key creates a stampede; single flight, TTL jitter and soft refresh bound the load on the database.
- Cache DTOs, not entities, and bound Redis timeouts so that a cache failure degrades latency instead of availability.

A Spring Boot application is delivered as an executable archive and, in most organisations, as a container image. The choices made at this stage (layer structure, base image, JVM memory flags, user, shutdown behaviour) decide build time, image size, start-up time, resource consumption and whether a deployment drops requests. This chapter explains the structure of the executable jar, builds an efficient image in two ways, sets JVM flags correctly for containers, and covers graceful shutdown and local development with Docker Compose. The JVM behaviour inside containers (cgroup limits, ergonomics) is covered in the operating-systems guide and is referenced here only by name.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The executable jar and layers

`mvn package` with the `spring-boot-maven-plugin` runs the `repackage` goal, which rewrites the plain jar into an executable archive: application classes under `BOOT-INF/classes`, dependency jars under `BOOT-INF/lib`, the launcher classes under `org/springframework/boot/loader`, and a manifest whose `Main-Class` is `JarLauncher` and whose `Start-Class` is the application class. Nested jars are not supported by the standard class loader, which is why `JarLauncher` installs its own `LaunchedURLClassLoader`.

The archive also contains `BOOT-INF/layers.idx`, which assigns every file to a layer: `dependencies` (released dependencies), `spring-boot-loader`, `snapshot-dependencies` and `application`. Docker caches an image layer as long as the instruction and its input are unchanged. If the entire fat jar is one `COPY` layer, a one-line code change invalidates the full 40 MB (typical size) layer; with extracted layers only the `application` layer, a few hundred kilobytes, changes.

blocks.text:
Spring Boot 3.3 introduced the `tools` jar mode (`java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --layers` `--destination extracted`) as the replacement of the older `layertools` mode. The extracted application starts with `java -jar application.jar` from the extraction directory; the jar then contains only application classes and references its dependencies through the manifest class path, which is also the layout recommended for class-data sharing and the ahead-of-time cache.

#### Two ways to build an image

**Dockerfile.** Full control and the most transparent option. A multi-stage build uses a JDK image to extract the layers and a JRE image to run them.

**Cloud Native Buildpacks.** `mvn spring-boot:build-image` (or `gradle bootBuildImage`) runs the Paketo Java buildpack through the Docker daemon. It selects a JRE, creates layers, configures the memory calculator, and sets a non-root user. No Dockerfile is written. The cost is less control and a requirement for a Docker daemon at build time.

### Worked example

blocks.code:
# ---------- stage 1: extract layers ----------
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS builder
WORKDIR /builder
ARG JAR_FILE=target/*.jar
COPY ${JAR_FILE} application.jar
RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar application.jar extract --layers --destination extracted

# ---------- stage 2: runtime ----------
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
WORKDIR /application

RUN groupadd --system --gid 10001 app \
 && useradd --system --uid 10001 --gid app --no-create-home app

COPY --from=builder /builder/extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /builder/extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=builder /builder/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /builder/extracted/application/ ./

USER 10001:10001
EXPOSE 8080
ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError"
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "application.jar"]
blocks.title: Dockerfile

blocks.text: The instruction order is the layer order: dependencies first because they change least. `USER 10001:10001` makes the process run as a numeric non-root user, which Kubernetes `runAsNonRoot` verifies without needing to resolve a name. The base image tags should be pinned further than `21-jre` in production (for example by digest) so that rebuilds are reproducible. The structure follows the Spring Boot reference Dockerfile; the base image there is a Liberica JRE and the one here is Eclipse Temurin.

blocks.text:
### JVM flags and memory in containers

Since JDK 10 the JVM reads the cgroup limits of the container. Without flags, the maximum heap is 25 per cent of the container limit (`MaxRAMPercentage` default 25), which wastes memory in a container that holds only one JVM. `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75` is a common starting point for containers of 1 GiB or more; for smaller limits a lower percentage is needed because non-heap memory is a larger fraction.

Heap is only part of the footprint. The process also needs metaspace, the code cache, thread stacks (default 1 MiB each on 64-bit Linux, and a Tomcat of 200 threads can reserve 200 MiB), direct buffers (NIO, Netty, Kafka client), GC data structures and native allocator overhead. The Paketo memory calculator computes `-Xmx` from the container limit after subtracting estimates for those areas (thread count default 250, class count from the jar) and writes the flags into `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`; with a hand-written Dockerfile the sizing is the operator's task.

blocks.text: Useful flags:

rows: maximum heap as a fraction of the container memory limit
terminate on OutOfMemoryError so that the orchestrator restarts a clean process
write a heap dump; needs a writable volume and enough disk
enable native memory accounting for jcmd VM.native\_memory
smaller thread stacks when thread counts are high
the JVM selects Serial GC under 2 CPUs or 1792 MiB of memory; G1 otherwise
blocks.caption: JVM flags for containerised Spring Boot services (JDK 21).

blocks.text:
The last row reflects the JVM ergonomics rule that a machine with fewer than two available processors or less than about 1792 MiB of memory is classified as not a server-class machine and gets the serial collector; the choice should be verified with `java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version` inside the actual container.

### Graceful shutdown

When Kubernetes (or `docker stop`) terminates a container, it sends `SIGTERM`, waits for the grace period, then sends `SIGKILL`. Without special handling, Tomcat stops immediately and in-flight requests receive connection resets. With `server.shutdown=graceful` the embedded web server stops accepting new connections, lets active requests finish, and the application context closes afterwards; the wait is bounded by `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase` (default 30 s). The behaviour is implemented by `SmartLifecycle` beans that are stopped in phases: the web server's graceful shutdown phase runs before the closing of beans such as data sources.

blocks.code:
server:
  shutdown: graceful
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 25s
blocks.title: application.yml (fragment)

blocks.text: The principle can be demonstrated with the JDK HTTP server: a handler takes one second, the server is stopped 300 ms after the request starts, once with `stop(0)` (immediate) and once with `stop(5)` (wait up to five seconds for exchanges to finish).

blocks.title: Graceful.java

blocks.code:
$ java Graceful.java
stop(0): in-flight request -> client error: IOException
stop(5): in-flight request -> HTTP 200 done
blocks.title: Output of the shutdown simulation (run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
An immediate stop cuts the in-flight exchange and the client sees an `IOException`; a stop with a delay lets the request complete with status 200. Spring Boot applies the same idea at the framework level.

Kubernetes adds a second problem: removing the pod from the Service endpoints and delivering `SIGTERM` happen concurrently, so a few requests can still be routed to a pod that has begun shutting down. A `preStop` hook with a short sleep (5 s) delays the signal until endpoint propagation has completed. The grace period must exceed the preStop sleep plus the shutdown timeout, or the container receives `SIGKILL` first.

### Local development with Docker Compose

A compose file defines the backing services of the application for local work.

blocks.code:
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: orders
      POSTGRES_USER: orders
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: orders
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U orders -d orders"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

  redis:
    image: redis:7
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"

  kafka:
    image: apache/kafka:3.8.0
    ports:
      - "9092:9092"
    environment:
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 1
      KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: broker,controller
      KAFKA_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://:9092,CONTROLLER://:9093
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://localhost:9092
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_LISTENER_NAMES: CONTROLLER
      KAFKA_LISTENER_SECURITY_PROTOCOL_MAP: CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT,PLAINTEXT:PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_QUORUM_VOTERS: 1@localhost:9093
      KAFKA_OFFSETS_TOPIC_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_MIN_ISR: 1

volumes:
  pgdata:
blocks.title: compose.yaml

blocks.text:
The single-node KRaft configuration is for development only. With the dependency `spring-boot-docker-compose` (Maven `optional`, Gradle `developmentOnly`), Spring Boot 3.1 and later finds `compose.yaml` in the working directory, runs `docker compose up` at startup, and creates connection details for recognised images, so that `spring.datasource.url` and `spring.data.redis.port` need not be configured. Matching is by image name (`postgres`, `redis`, and a list of other databases and brokers; the reference documentation lists which Kafka images are recognised for the Boot version in use). The relevant properties are `spring.docker.compose.file`, `spring.docker.compose.lifecycle-management` (`none`, `start-only`, `start-and-stop`) and `spring.docker.compose.skip.in-tests` (Compose support is off in tests by default). Services that are already running are reused.

For tests, Testcontainers with `@ServiceConnection` (Boot 3.1 and later) fills the same role; the testing part of this guide covers it.

### Hands-on

$ docker build -t orders:dev .
$ docker images orders:dev --format '{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}}  {{.Size}}'

blocks.title: typical output (not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
After editing one controller and rebuilding, `docker build` reports `CACHED` for the layers up to `dependencies`, and `docker` `push` uploads only the changed `application` layer.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: container killed with OOMKilled while the heap is healthy

**Scenario.** A service with a 1 GiB memory limit restarts every few hours; Grafana shows the JVM heap at 450 MiB of 768 MiB just before each restart. **Symptoms.** `kubectl get pod` shows `RESTARTS` increasing; `kubectl describe pod` shows `Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137`; the application log ends without an exception. **Diagnosis.** The kernel killed the process, so no Java diagnostics exist. Check `container_memory_working_set_bytes` against the limit. Start the container with `-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary` and run `jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory` `summary` after some hours; compare `Thread`, `Class`, `Code`, `Internal` and `Other` against the plan. Count threads with `jcmd` `<pid> Thread.print | grep -c '"'`. **Root cause.** `MaxRAMPercentage=75` assumed 25 per cent for everything else, but 400 request threads (400 MiB reserved stack), 120 MiB metaspace and 80 MiB of direct buffers from the Kafka client exceeded it. **Fix.** Lower the heap fraction (60 per cent), cap Tomcat threads (`server.tomcat.threads.max=100`) or use virtual threads, set `-Xss512k`, limit direct memory (`-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize`), or raise the container limit. **Prevention.** Budget memory as the sum of its parts, load-test at the container limit, and alert on `working_set /` `limit` above 85 per cent.

#### Problem 2: image is large and builds are slow

**Scenario.** A pipeline takes nine minutes, of which six are image build and push; the image is 780 MB. **Symptoms.** Every push uploads the full image; the registry is slow; pulls on new nodes take a minute. **Diagnosis.** `docker history` `<image>` shows one 560 MB layer for the jar copy and a JDK base image; `docker image ls` shows the size; `dive` can show layer content. **Root cause.** The Dockerfile copies the fat jar in one layer and uses a full JDK image as the runtime stage. **Fix.** Multi-stage build with layer extraction and a JRE base image; `.dockerignore` for `target/` history and `.git`; remove unused starters and dependencies (`mvn dependency:tree`, `mvn dependency:analyze`); for fast start-up consider the AOT cache or CDS. **Prevention.** Track image size in the pipeline and fail on a growth threshold.

#### Problem 3: requests fail during a deployment

**Scenario.** Every rolling update produces a burst of 502 responses at the ingress for about three seconds, plus a few client-visible connection resets. **Symptoms.** 502/503 spikes aligned with deployments; no errors in the application log. **Diagnosis.** Compare the timestamps of the 502s with pod termination events (`kubectl get events` `--sort-by=.lastTimestamp`); check `server.shutdown` in the effective configuration (`/actuator/configprops` or `/actuator/env`); check `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`. **Root cause.** `server.shutdown` was `immediate` (the default), and there was no `preStop` delay, so endpoints still pointed at a terminating pod. **Fix.** `server.shutdown=graceful`, a `preStop` sleep of 5 seconds, `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` larger than the sum of that sleep and the shutdown timeout, and a readiness probe that turns `OUT_OF_SERVICE` during shutdown (Boot does this when probes are enabled). **Prevention.** A deployment test that runs a constant request stream during a rollout and asserts zero errors.

### Questions to expect

1. **Why layered jars?** Layers separate rarely changing dependencies from frequently changing application classes so that Docker caches and registries transfer only what changed.
2. **Dockerfile or buildpacks?** Dockerfiles give full control and transparency; buildpacks give secure, consistent defaults without maintaining a Dockerfile but need a Docker daemon and offer less tailoring.
3. **What does** `MaxRAMPercentage` **do and why is 75 not always safe?** It sets the maximum heap as a percentage of the container limit. Non-heap memory (stacks, metaspace, direct buffers) can exceed the remaining 25 per cent in thread-heavy services.
4. **What is exit code 137?** The process received `SIGKILL` (128 + 9); in Kubernetes with `OOMKilled` it was the kernel out-of-memory killer.
5. **How does graceful shutdown work in Spring Boot?** `server.shutdown=graceful` stops accepting new requests and waits for active ones for up to `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase` before the context closes.
6. **Why run the container as non-root?** A compromise of the application then has no root privileges inside the container, which limits escape and file system damage; Kubernetes can enforce it with `runAsNonRoot`.
7. **Why a multi-stage build?** The build tools and the JDK stay in the first stage; only runtime files are in the final image, which is smaller and has a smaller attack surface.
8. **How is configuration supplied to a container?** Through environment variables (relaxed binding maps `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` to `spring.datasource.url`), mounted files and `spring.config.import`; never baked into the image.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Layered extraction and a JRE runtime stage give small, cache-friendly images; a non-root numeric user is the default.

- Heap is only part of container memory; budget stacks, metaspace, direct buffers and native memory, or the kernel kills the process with exit code 137.
- `server.shutdown=graceful`, a `preStop` delay and a sufficient `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` are all required for zero-error rollouts.
- Docker Compose with Spring Boot's Compose support, or Testcontainers with `@ServiceConnection`, replaces manual configuration of local backing services.

Kubernetes runs containers, restarts them when they fail, routes traffic to the healthy ones and replaces them gradually during a release. A Spring developer does not need to administer a cluster, but must understand the objects that determine whether an application starts, receives traffic, scales and shuts down correctly. Most production incidents involving Spring Boot on Kubernetes are interactions between application behaviour (start-up time, memory use, shutdown) and platform behaviour (probes, limits, rolling updates). The YAML in this chapter is typical configuration and was not applied to a cluster on the build machine.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The objects

A **Pod** is one or more containers sharing a network namespace; it is the unit of scheduling and is disposable. A **Deployment** declares the desired number of identical pods and an update strategy; it manages **ReplicaSets**, one per pod template version. A **Service** gives a set of pods (selected by labels) a stable virtual IP and DNS name (`orders.shop.svc.cluster.local`) and load-balances over the ready ones. An **Ingress** routes external HTTP(S) requests by host and path to services, through an ingress controller such as ingress-nginx. A **ConfigMap** holds non-sensitive configuration and a **Secret** holds sensitive values (stored base64-encoded, which is an encoding and not encryption; encryption at rest and RBAC must be configured on the cluster). Both are injected as environment variables or mounted as files.

blocks.text:
#### Probes

Three probes tell the kubelet what to do with a container:

- The **startup probe** runs until it first succeeds; liveness and readiness probes are disabled until then. It covers slow start-up without making the liveness probe lenient forever.
- The **liveness probe** answers "is the process unrecoverably broken?". Failure makes the kubelet restart the container.
- The **readiness probe** answers "can this pod serve traffic now?". Failure removes the pod from the Service endpoints without restarting it.

Spring Boot Actuator provides two health groups for this purpose: `/actuator/health/liveness` (state `LivenessState`, `CORRECT` or `BROKEN`) and `/actuator/health/readiness` (state `ReadinessState`, `ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC` or `REFUSING_TRAFFIC`). They are enabled automatically when Boot detects Kubernetes through the `*_SERVICE_HOST` and `*_SERVICE_PORT` environment variables, and explicitly with `management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true`. During graceful shutdown the readiness state changes to `REFUSING_TRAFFIC` first. The liveness group should not include external dependencies such as the database: if the database is down, restarting every pod does not help and turns an incident into a restart storm. The readiness group may include them.

#### Resources

Each container has `requests` (the amount the scheduler reserves, and the CPU share under contention) and `limits` (the cap). A memory limit is enforced by the kernel: exceeding it ends in `OOMKilled`. A CPU limit is enforced by throttling via the CFS quota; a JVM that starts with a CPU limit of 500m is throttled during class loading and JIT compilation, so start-up takes several times longer than with a larger limit, which can fail the probes. The JVM sizes its default thread pools and GC threads from the CPU limit it sees.

#### Rolling updates

A Deployment with `strategy.type: RollingUpdate` replaces pods gradually. `maxSurge` is the number of extra pods allowed above the desired count and `maxUnavailable` the number of pods that may be unavailable. With `maxSurge: 1` and `maxUnavailable: 0`, a new pod is created, and only when its readiness probe succeeds is an old pod terminated. The readiness probe is therefore the gate of the whole update.
