blocks.text: ### Worked example

blocks.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: orders-config
  namespace: shop
data:
  SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: "prod"
  SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: "jdbc:postgresql://postgres.shop.svc.cluster.local:5432/orders"
  SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: "orders"
  SPRING_KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS: "kafka.shop.svc.cluster.local:9092"
  SERVER_SHUTDOWN: "graceful"
  MANAGEMENT_ENDPOINT_HEALTH_PROBES_ENABLED: "true"
blocks.title: k8s/configmap.yaml

blocks.text: Relaxed binding maps the upper-case environment variable `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` to the property `spring.datasource.url`; underscores replace dots and hyphens.

blocks.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: orders-secret
  namespace: shop
type: Opaque
stringData:
  SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: "change-me"
blocks.title: k8s/secret.yaml

blocks.text: This file is a template. A real value is never committed; it is created by a secret manager integration (External Secrets Operator, Sealed Secrets, a CSI driver) or by the pipeline from a protected store.

blocks.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders
  namespace: shop
  labels:
    app: orders
spec:
  replicas: 3
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  template:
metadata:
  labels:
    app: orders
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 10001
  containers:
    - name: orders
      image: registry.example.com/shop/orders:1.4.2
      ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
          name: http
      envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: orders-config
        - secretRef:
            name: orders-secret
      env:
        - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
          value: "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError"
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: "500m"
          memory: "768Mi"
        limits:
          memory: "1Gi"
      startupProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /actuator/health/liveness
          port: http
        periodSeconds: 5
        failureThreshold: 30
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /actuator/health/liveness
          port: http
        periodSeconds: 10
        failureThreshold: 3
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /actuator/health/readiness
          port: http
        periodSeconds: 5
        failureThreshold: 3
      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          exec:
            command: ["sleep", "5"]
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      volumeMounts:
        - name: tmp
          mountPath: /tmp
  volumes:
    - name: tmp
      emptyDir: {}
blocks.title: k8s/deployment.yaml

blocks.text: What to notice: the memory request is below the limit but the CPU limit is omitted on purpose (a request without a limit avoids throttling while still reserving capacity; the policy is a team decision); the startup probe allows 30 x 5 s = 150 s for start-up before liveness takes over; the `preStop` sleep of 5 s plus a shutdown timeout of 25 s is below `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45`; `readOnlyRootFilesystem` requires a writable `/tmp`, which Tomcat and the JVM use for working files; and the heap fraction (70 per cent of 1 GiB) leaves 300 MiB for non-heap memory.

blocks.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders
  namespace: shop
spec:
  selector:
    app: orders
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: orders
  namespace: shop
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "30"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts: ["api.example.com"]
      secretName: api-example-com-tls
  rules:
    - host: api.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /orders
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: orders
                port:
                  name: http
blocks.title: k8s/service-ingress.yaml

blocks.code:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: orders
  namespace: shop
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: orders
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: orders
  namespace: shop
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders
blocks.title: k8s/hpa-pdb.yaml

blocks.text:
The HPA computes utilisation relative to the CPU **request**, so the request must be realistic: a request of 500m and an average usage of 350m is 70 per cent. The `PodDisruptionBudget` limits voluntary evictions (node drains) so that at least two replicas stay available.

#### Helm basics

Helm packages the manifests as a chart: `Chart.yaml` (name, version), `values.yaml` (defaults) and `templates/` (manifests with Go templating). A release is created or upgraded with one command, and the previous revision can be restored.

blocks.code:
replicaCount: 3
image:
  repository: registry.example.com/shop/orders
  tag: "1.4.2"
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 768Mi
  limits:
    memory: 1Gi
blocks.title: values.yaml (fragment)

blocks.text: **templates/deployment.yaml (fragment)**

blocks.code:
$ helm upgrade --install orders ./chart -n shop --set image.tag=1.4.3 --atomic --timeout 5m
$ helm history orders -n shop
$ helm rollback orders 3 -n shop
blocks.title: typical commands (not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
`--atomic` rolls the release back automatically if the pods do not become ready within the timeout.

### Hands-on

$ kubectl -n shop get pods -l app=orders
NAME                      READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
orders-6d9c7b5f64-4kq2x   1/1     Running   0          2m
orders-6d9c7b5f64-9tz7p   1/1     Running   0          98s

blocks.text:
### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: rolling update stalls, new pods never become ready

**Scenario.** A new version is deployed; `kubectl rollout status` waits indefinitely, while the old pods keep serving. **Symptoms.** New pods show `0/1 Running`; `READY` never turns to `1/1`; the progress deadline (600 s by default) eventually marks the rollout `ProgressDeadlineExceeded`. **Diagnosis.** `kubectl describe pod <new>` lists `Readiness` `probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503` or `connection refused` in Events. `kubectl logs <new>` shows whether the application started. `kubectl exec <new> -- curl -s` `localhost:8080/actuator/health/readiness` (or `wget`) shows the group state and, with `management.endpoint.health.show-details=always`, the failing component. **Root cause.** Three typical causes. The readiness group included `db`, and the new configuration pointed to an unreachable host. The probe port was 8080 while the management server had been moved to `management.server.port=9090`. The probe period was too short for a pod that had only 200m of CPU, so the start-up took 70 seconds and `failureThreshold` was reached. **Fix.** Correct the configuration; align the probe port with `management.server.port`; add a `startupProbe` with a generous `failureThreshold`; raise the CPU request. The old pods keep serving because `maxUnavailable: 0`, which is the reason the readiness gate exists. Roll back with `kubectl rollout undo` if the cause is not immediate. **Prevention.** Run the same image with the production profile in a staging namespace before production; use `helm --atomic`; keep the liveness group free of external dependencies.

#### Problem 2: liveness probe kills a pod that is merely slow

**Scenario.** During a traffic peak pods restart in sequence, which reduces capacity and amplifies the load on the others. **Symptoms.** `RESTARTS` increases on all pods within minutes; the log ends at an arbitrary point; `describe` shows `Liveness probe failed: context deadline exceeded`. **Diagnosis.** The Tomcat thread pool is saturated (metric `tomcat.threads.busy` equals `tomcat.threads.config.max`), so the health request waits in the accept queue and exceeds the probe `timeoutSeconds` (1 s default). **Root cause.** The probe shares the thread pool with business traffic, and the liveness probe tests responsiveness instead of broken state. **Fix.** Serve Actuator on a separate management port (`management.server.port`), which uses its own connector and thread pool; raise `timeoutSeconds` and `failureThreshold` of liveness; leave overload to readiness and load shedding. **Prevention.** Treat liveness as "restart will help" only; a slow application should shed load, not restart.

#### Problem 3: very slow start-up under a CPU limit

**Scenario.** A service that starts in 12 seconds on a developer laptop takes 95 seconds in the cluster with a CPU limit of 500m. **Symptoms.** Restart loops caused by failing probes; the log timestamps show class loading and bean creation spread over minutes. **Diagnosis.** `container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total` is high during start-up; `kubectl top` `pod` shows usage pinned at the limit. **Root cause.** The JIT compiler and class loading are CPU-bound and are throttled by the CFS quota. **Fix.** Raise the CPU limit or remove it while keeping a request; add a startup probe; reduce start-up work (lazy initialisation, fewer auto-configurations); use the AOT cache or CDS where the JDK supports it. **Prevention.** Measure start-up in a container with the production limits.

### Questions to expect

1. **What is the difference between liveness and readiness?** Liveness failure restarts the container; readiness failure removes the pod from Service endpoints without a restart. Liveness should detect an unrecoverable state, readiness an inability to serve.
2. **What does the startup probe add?** It suspends the other probes until the application has started, which allows slow starts without weakening liveness.
3. **How does Spring Boot support the probes?** The Actuator health groups `liveness` and `readiness`, backed by `ApplicationAvailability` states, enabled automatically on Kubernetes.
4. **What are requests and limits?** Requests are reserved for scheduling; limits are enforced caps. Exceeding the memory limit kills the container; exceeding the CPU limit throttles it.
5. **Explain a rolling update.** The Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and scales it up while scaling the old one down within `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable`, gated by readiness.
6. **How does the HPA decide to scale?** It compares the observed average metric (for example CPU utilisation relative to the request) with the target and adjusts the replica count between the minimum and maximum.
7. **How are secrets handled?** As Secret objects injected as environment variables or files, with encryption at rest, RBAC and preferably an external secret store; never in the image or the repository.
8. **Why is a preStop hook used?** Endpoint removal and `SIGTERM` are concurrent; a short sleep lets traffic drain before the application stops accepting connections.
9. **ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer?** ClusterIP exposes inside the cluster, NodePort on each node's port, LoadBalancer provisions a cloud load balancer; Ingress adds HTTP routing on top.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
The readiness probe gates both traffic and rolling updates; the liveness probe must not depend on external systems.

- Memory limits kill (OOMKilled), CPU limits throttle (slow start-up); requests drive scheduling and HPA arithmetic.
- Graceful shutdown needs `server.shutdown=graceful`, a preStop delay and a grace period longer than both.
- Configuration comes from ConfigMaps and Secrets through relaxed binding of environment variables; no secrets in images or repositories.

Continuous integration builds and tests every change automatically; continuous delivery keeps the main branch always releasable and automates the path to production. For a Spring Boot service the pipeline compiles with Maven, runs unit and integration tests (the latter with Testcontainers), scans dependencies and the image, builds and pushes the image, and deploys it with a strategy that limits the damage of a faulty release. The pipeline is part of the product: a flaky pipeline stops delivery, and a leaked credential in a pipeline is an incident. The YAML in this chapter is typical GitHub Actions configuration and was not executed on the build machine.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Maven essentials

Maven builds by walking a **lifecycle** of phases. The default lifecycle contains, in order, `validate`, `compile`, `test`, `package`, `verify`, `install` and `deploy`; invoking a phase runs all earlier phases. Plugins bind **goals** to phases: `maven-compiler-plugin:compile` to `compile`, `maven-surefire-plugin:test` to `test`, `maven-failsafe-plugin` to `integration-test` and `verify`, and the `spring-boot-maven-plugin:repackage` goal to `package`. CI normally runs `mvn` `-B clean verify`: batch mode without colour or interactive prompts, and no `install` or `deploy` of artefacts into repositories.

blocks.text:
**Dependency management.** `spring-boot-starter-parent` (or the `spring-boot-dependencies` BOM imported in `dependencyManagement`) fixes the versions of several hundred libraries to a mutually tested set; dependencies declared without a `version` take the managed version. An override of a managed version is done with a property such as `<jackson-bom.version>` in the properties of the project and requires care, because the set was tested as a whole. Scopes: `compile` (default), `provided` (needed at compile time only, for example servlet API when deploying to a container), `runtime`, `test`. Transitive dependencies are resolved by nearest definition; `mvn dependency:tree` shows the resolved tree and `-Dverbose` shows conflicts.

**Surefire and Failsafe.** Surefire runs unit tests (classes named `*Test`, `Test*`, `*Tests`, `*TestCase`) in the `test` phase. Failsafe runs integration tests (`*IT`, `IT*`, `*ITCase`) in `integration-test` and checks the results in `verify`, so that cleanup in `post-integration-test` runs even when a test fails. Separating them gives a fast first feedback stage.

**Profiles** activate sets of configuration by command line (`-Pnative`), property, JDK or environment. They are appropriate for build variants; runtime configuration belongs to Spring profiles (`spring.profiles.active`), not Maven profiles, because a Maven profile bakes the choice into the artefact and the same artefact should run in every environment.

<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.4.1</version>
    <relativePath/>
</parent>

<properties>
    <java.version>21</java.version>
</properties>

<build>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
        </plugin>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
            <artifactId>maven-failsafe-plugin</artifactId>
            <executions>
                <execution>
                    <goals>
                        <goal>integration-test</goal>
                        <goal>verify</goal>
                    </goals>
                </execution>
            </executions>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>

blocks.text:
The version numbers of Maven plugins that appear without a version in this fragment are managed by the parent. The Boot version in the example is illustrative; the project pins the current patch release of the supported 3.x line.

#### Versioning and artefacts

The pipeline builds the artefact once and promotes the same image through environments; rebuilding per environment defeats the purpose of testing it. The image tag is immutable and traceable: the Git commit SHA (`orders:3f9c2d1`) for every build and a semantic version (`1.4.2`) for releases. The mutable tag `latest` is avoided in deployments because it cannot be rolled back deterministically and gives no information about what runs. Semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) applies to libraries and to public API contracts; for deployed services the commit SHA is usually the real identity.

### Worked example

blocks.code:
name: ci

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    tags: ["v*"]

permissions:
  contents: read

env:
  REGISTRY: registry.example.com
  IMAGE: registry.example.com/shop/orders

jobs:
  build-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: "21"
          cache: maven
      - name: Build, unit tests, integration tests (Testcontainers)
        run: ./mvnw -B clean verify
      - name: Upload test reports
        if: failure()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: surefire-reports
          path: |
            target/surefire-reports
            target/failsafe-reports
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: app-jar
          path: target/*.jar

  image:
    needs: build-test
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: app-jar
          path: target
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}
          username: ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_USER }}
          password: ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ env.IMAGE }}:${{ github.sha }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max
      - name: Scan image for known vulnerabilities
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@0.28.0
        with:
          image-ref: ${{ env.IMAGE }}:${{ github.sha }}
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
          exit-code: "1"
        ignore-unfixed: true

deploy-staging:
  needs: image
  if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  environment: staging
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - name: Deploy with Helm
      run: |
        helm upgrade --install orders ./chart -n shop-staging \
          --set image.tag=${{ github.sha }} --atomic --timeout 5m
blocks.title: .github/workflows/ci.yml

blocks.text: What to notice. The `permissions` block starts at read-only and widens per job. Pull requests run only the `build-test` job; images are built and pushed only on pushes to `main` or tags. The same jar produced by the verified build is reused for the image. The environment `staging` can hold its own secrets and protection rules, and a production job would use an environment with required reviewers (manual approval). The cluster credentials are supplied through the environment's secrets or, better, through short-lived OIDC federation (`id-token: write`) instead of a long-lived kubeconfig. Third-party actions should be pinned to a specific version or commit SHA; the versions in the example are illustrative and must be checked when the workflow is written.

blocks.text:
### Release strategies

**Rolling update.** The default in Kubernetes: replace pods gradually. Two versions serve traffic concurrently, so every change must be backward compatible with the previous version, especially the database schema and message formats.

**Blue-green.** Two complete environments exist; traffic is switched from the live one (blue) to the new one (green) at the router or service selector. Rollback is switching back. The cost is double capacity, and the database must be compatible with both versions.

**Canary.** A small fraction of traffic (5 per cent) goes to the new version while error rate and latency are compared with the stable version; the share grows step by step or the canary is rolled back. It needs traffic splitting (ingress annotations, a service mesh, Argo Rollouts) and metrics-based analysis, and gives the smallest blast radius.

blocks.text:
**Feature flags.** A flag separates deployment from release: the code ships switched off and is enabled per user, tenant or percentage at runtime (a library such as FF4j or Unleash, or a simple `@ConfigurationProperties` toggle backed by a refreshable config source). Flags need an owner and a removal date; stale flags are untested code paths.

**Database migrations in the pipeline.** Schema changes follow the expand-and-contract pattern so that old and new application versions work against the same schema. Step one adds a nullable column or a new table (expand) with Flyway or Liquibase running at application start or as a separate migration job before the rollout; step two deploys code that writes both and reads the new structure; step three, one release later, drops the old column (contract). A destructive migration in the same release as the code that stops using the column breaks a rolling update, because old pods still use it. A migration that locks a large table (an `ALTER TABLE` with a rewrite, an index created without `CONCURRENTLY` in PostgreSQL) can block the whole service; it requires a dedicated procedure.

**Secrets management.** Credentials enter the pipeline and the runtime through a secret store (GitHub environment secrets, HashiCorp Vault, a cloud secret manager) and are rotated. They never appear in the repository, image layers, build logs or `docker history`. Secret scanning (GitHub secret scanning, gitleaks) runs on every push, and any committed secret is treated as compromised and rotated regardless of removal from history.

### Hands-on

A local reproduction of the CI build, the commands that the workflow runs:

blocks.text:
### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: the pipeline is flaky because of Testcontainers

**Scenario.** About one build in ten fails in the integration stage with `Could not start container` or `Connection` `refused`, and passes on re-run. **Symptoms.** Failures are not tied to code changes; the logs show timeouts waiting for PostgreSQL or Kafka; sometimes `no space left on device`. **Diagnosis.** Read the Testcontainers log lines (`Waiting` `for database connection to become available`) and the elapsed time per test class; run `docker system df` on the runner; check whether several test classes each start their own container; check the registry for rate-limit errors (`toomanyrequests`) in the image pull. **Root cause.** Each test class started its own PostgreSQL container, producing 25 containers per build on a shared two-core runner; image pulls from a public registry were rate limited; the default startup timeout was exceeded under load. **Fix.** Share one container per JVM with a singleton or `@ServiceConnection` bean in a shared `@TestConfiguration`; enable the Spring test context cache by using identical configuration; pre-pull images from a mirror or the organisation's registry; raise the startup timeout (`withStartupTimeout`) and use wait strategies instead of sleeps; prune images on the runner. **Prevention.** Track test duration and failure rate per test class; quarantine and fix flaky tests, not retry them silently.

#### Problem 2: a secret is committed to the repository

**Scenario.** A developer commits `application-prod.yml` containing the database password and a cloud access key; the push succeeds and the repository is visible to the whole organisation (and, in the worst case, public). **Symptoms.** A secret scanning alert, or unexpected usage of the key (billing anomaly, access from unknown addresses). **Diagnosis.** `git log -p --all -S'AKIA'` or a scanner (`gitleaks detect`) locates the commit; the provider's audit log shows use of the credential since the commit time. **Root cause.** Secrets were kept in a file in the repository, `.gitignore` did not exclude it, and no push protection existed. **Fix.** Revoke and rotate the credential first, since history rewriting does not undo exposure; then remove the file and, if required by policy, rewrite history (`git filter-repo`) and invalidate forks and caches. Move values to environment variables resolved from a secret manager (`spring.config.import=optional:configtree:/etc/secrets/` for mounted secrets, or `${DB_PASSWORD}` placeholders). **Prevention.** Enable push protection and secret scanning, add a pre-commit hook (gitleaks), keep only `application.yml` with placeholders in the repository, and grant cloud credentials short lifetimes through OIDC.

#### Problem 3: the release breaks the running version during the rolling update

**Scenario.** A migration renames a column in the same release as the code that reads the new name. During the rollout, old pods throw `column "customer_name" does not exist`. **Symptoms.** A burst of 500 responses from old pods during the update; the new pods are healthy. **Diagnosis.** The error log of the old pods shows the SQL error with the time of the Flyway migration; the `flyway_schema_history` table shows the version applied at that time. **Root cause.** The migration was not backward compatible with the version still serving traffic. **Fix.** Roll back the application and apply expand-and-contract: add `full_name`, write both columns, backfill, switch reads in the next release, drop the old column in a later one. **Prevention.** A pipeline test that runs the previous version's integration tests against the migrated schema.

### Questions to expect

1. **What are the Maven lifecycle phases?** `validate`, `compile`, `test`, `package`, `verify`, `install`, `deploy` in the default lifecycle; running a phase runs the earlier ones. Plugins bind goals to phases.
2. **What is a BOM?** A POM whose `dependencyManagement` section declares compatible versions; importing it (or inheriting `spring-boot-starter-parent`) lets dependencies omit versions.
3. **Surefire versus Failsafe?** Surefire runs unit tests in `test`; Failsafe runs integration tests in `integration-test` and fails the build in `verify`, after cleanup.
4. **How should images be tagged?** By immutable identifiers (commit SHA, release version) and never deployed by `latest`; one artefact is promoted through the environments.
5. **Blue-green versus canary?** Blue-green switches all traffic between two full environments with instant rollback; canary shifts a fraction progressively with metric analysis.
6. **What is expand-and-contract?** A migration approach in which the schema is first extended compatibly, the code is migrated, and the old structure is removed in a later release, so that two application versions can run concurrently.
7. **How are secrets kept out of a pipeline?** In a secret store, injected at runtime as environment secrets or via OIDC federation, scanned for leaks, rotated, and never echoed into logs.
8. **How is a flaky test handled?** Reproduce and fix the cause (shared state, time, ordering, resources); quarantine with a ticket; never rely on blind retries.
9. **Why build the artefact once?** The tested binary is the one deployed; rebuilding can include different dependencies or timestamps.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
The pipeline builds once, tests at several levels, scans, publishes an immutable image and promotes it; pull requests run the fast stages only.

- `mvn -B clean verify` runs unit tests with Surefire and integration tests with Failsafe; the Spring Boot BOM manages dependency versions.
- Rolling, blue-green and canary releases all require backward-compatible schemas and messages; expand-and-contract migrations make that possible.
- A committed secret is compromised and must be rotated; prevention is push protection, scanning and short-lived credentials.

The questions below cover the topics of the whole guide, grouped by area. The answers are model answers of two to five lines: a complete spoken answer starts with the mechanism, names the real classes or properties, and ends with a trade-off or a pitfall. A candidate should be able to produce the first sentence of each answer from memory and extend it with the mechanism when the interviewer probes. The chapter on the study plan maps these areas to a six-week schedule.

### Container, AOP and auto-configuration

1. **What is the difference between** `BeanFactory` **and** `ApplicationContext`**?** `BeanFactory` is the minimal container (`DefaultListableBeanFactory` is the implementation) that creates beans lazily on request. `ApplicationContext` adds eager singleton initialisation, event publication, message resources, environment and profiles, and automatic registration of `BeanPostProcessor` and `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` beans.
2. **Describe the bean creation sequence.** Instantiate (constructor), populate properties (injection), `Aware` callbacks, `BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization`, `@PostConstruct` and `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet`, custom init method, `postProcessAfterInitialization` (where AOP proxies are created), then use; on shutdown `@PreDestroy`, `DisposableBean`, destroy method.
3. `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` **versus** `BeanPostProcessor`**?** The first modifies bean definitions before any bean is instantiated (for example `PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer`, `ConfigurationClassPostProcessor`). The second wraps or modifies bean instances during creation (for example `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor`, the auto-proxy creators).
4. **How are circular dependencies handled?** Singleton setter or field injection is resolved with the three-level cache (`singletonObjects`, `earlySingletonObjects`, `singletonFactories`), exposing an early reference. Constructor injection cannot be resolved and fails with `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException`. Since Spring Boot 2.6 circular references are prohibited by default (`spring.main.allow-circular-references`), and the correct fix is to remove the cycle.
5. **Constructor, setter or field injection?** Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit and final, allows plain unit tests without a container and detects cycles at start-up. Setter injection fits optional dependencies. Field injection hides dependencies and prevents immutability.
6. **How does Spring resolve two beans of the same type?** By `@Primary`, then `@Qualifier`, then by matching the parameter name with the bean name; otherwise `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`.
7. **What are the bean scopes?** `singleton` (default, one per container), `prototype`, and in web applications `request`, `session`, `application`. A narrower scope injected into a singleton needs a scoped proxy (`proxyMode`) or `ObjectProvider`.
8. **JDK dynamic proxy versus CGLIB?** JDK proxies implement the interfaces of the target and use `InvocationHandler`. CGLIB (repackaged inside Spring, with Objenesis for instantiation) creates a subclass of the target class, so the class and the advised methods must not be `final`. Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB (`spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true`).
9. **Why does** `@Transactional` **not work on a self-invoked method?** The advice is applied by the proxy. A call through `this` goes directly to the target object and bypasses `TransactionInterceptor`. The same holds for `@Async`, `@Cacheable` and `@PreAuthorize`. Fix by moving the method to another bean or by injecting the proxy.
10. **What does** `@Configuration` **do differently from** `@Component`**?** A `@Configuration` class is CGLIB-proxied so that calls between its `@Bean` methods return the container's singleton instead of creating a new instance (full mode). With `proxyBeanMethods = false` (lite mode) the proxy is skipped, which speeds start-up but changes inter-bean method call behaviour.
11. **What is in** `@SpringBootApplication`**?** `@SpringBootConfiguration` (a `@Configuration`), `@EnableAutoConfiguration` (imports the candidates listed in `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`), and `@ComponentScan` of the package of the annotated class and its sub-packages.
12. **How does auto-configuration decide what to create?** Each auto-configuration class carries conditions: `@ConditionalOnClass`, `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`, `@ConditionalOnProperty` and others. A user-defined bean of the same type makes `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` back off. `--debug` prints the condition evaluation report.
13. **How is externalised configuration ordered?** Later sources win: default properties, `application.properties|yml` (profile-specific files over general ones), OS environment variables, Java system properties, command-line arguments (highest of the common ones). `@ConfigurationProperties` binds with relaxed rules (kebab, camel and upper-snake forms).
14. **How is a custom starter built?** An auto-configuration module with `@AutoConfiguration` classes, conditions and `@ConfigurationProperties`, registered in the `.imports` file, plus a starter module that depends on it.

### Spring MVC and HTTP clients

1. **Describe the lifecycle of a request in Spring MVC.** The servlet container passes the request through filters to `DispatcherServlet`. `HandlerMapping` (`RequestMappingHandlerMapping`) selects a handler, `HandlerAdapter` invokes it after argument resolution and `HttpMessageConverter` reading, the return value is written by a converter or rendered as a view, and interceptors run before and after.
2. **Filter versus** `HandlerInterceptor`**?** A filter belongs to the servlet container, wraps the whole chain including static resources and is independent of Spring MVC. An interceptor is part of MVC, runs around handler execution, and knows the matched handler.
3. `@Controller` **versus** `@RestController`**?** `@RestController` is `@Controller` plus `@ResponseBody`: return values are written through message converters instead of being resolved as view names.
4. **What causes 415, 406 and 400?** 415: no converter for the request `Content-Type`. 406: no converter satisfies the `Accept` header. 400: malformed JSON (`HttpMessageNotReadableException`), failed validation (`MethodArgumentNotValidException`) or a missing parameter.
5. **How is global error handling done?** `@RestControllerAdvice` with `@ExceptionHandler` methods; Spring 6 supports `ProblemDetail` (RFC 9457) responses, enabled for built-in exceptions with `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true`.
6. **What does** `@Valid` **do and what is** `@Validated`**?** `@Valid` triggers Bean Validation of the argument, producing `MethodArgumentNotValidException`. `@Validated` on a class enables method-level validation of parameters (constraint violations raise `ConstraintViolationException`) and supports validation groups.
7. **How many requests can a Boot web application serve concurrently?** With Tomcat the pool is `server.tomcat.threads.max` (default 200), one thread per request; beyond that requests wait in `accept-count` (100) and `max-connections` (8192 for NIO). With `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` on JDK 21 (Boot 3.2 and later), request handling uses virtual threads and the pool is no longer the limit; downstream pools become the limit.
8. **How do CORS preflights work?** A browser sends `OPTIONS` with `Origin` and `Access-Control-Request-Method` before a non-simple request; the server must answer with `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers. With Spring Security the CORS configuration must be applied before authorisation (`http.cors(...)`), otherwise the preflight is rejected with 401 or 403.
9. **How is pagination done in Spring Data and MVC?** A controller parameter of type `Pageable` is resolved from `page`, `size` and `sort`; the repository returns `Page<T>` (with a count query) or `Slice<T>` (without).
10. `RestTemplate`**,** `WebClient`**,** `RestClient` **and HTTP interfaces?** `RestTemplate` is blocking and in maintenance mode. `WebClient` is reactive and non-blocking. `RestClient` (Spring 6.1 and Boot 3.2) is a blocking fluent client that replaces `RestTemplate` in new code. `@HttpExchange` interfaces generate a client from an annotated interface on top of `RestClient` or `WebClient`.
11. **Which timeouts must every HTTP client set?** Connect timeout and read timeout (and a pool acquisition timeout). Without them a slow dependency holds threads indefinitely.
12. **What is** `ETag` **support in Spring MVC?** `ShallowEtagHeaderFilter` computes a hash of the response body and returns 304 for a matching `If-None-Match`; it saves bandwidth, not server work.

### JPA and Hibernate

1. **What is the persistence context?** The first-level cache and unit of work of an `EntityManager`: it tracks managed entities by identity, detects changes (dirty checking) at flush time and guarantees one instance per row per context.
2. **What are the entity states?** Transient (new), managed (attached), detached (was managed, context closed) and removed. `persist`, `merge`, `remove` and `detach` move between them.
3. **When does Hibernate flush?** Before a query that could be affected (`FlushModeType.AUTO`), at transaction commit, and on explicit `flush()`.
4. **What is the N+1 problem and how is it fixed?** One query loads N parents and a further N queries load each lazy association. Fix with `JOIN FETCH`, `@EntityGraph`, `@BatchSize`/`default_batch_fetch_size`, or a DTO projection.
5. `LAZY` **versus** `EAGER`**?** `LAZY` loads on first access through a proxy or collection wrapper; `EAGER` loads immediately and is a fixed global plan that is usually wrong. Associations should be `LAZY` and fetched per use case.
6. **What causes** `LazyInitializationException`**?** Access to an uninitialised proxy or collection after the persistence context was closed. Fetch what the view needs inside the transaction, or map to DTOs there; open-in-view only hides it.
7. **What is open-in-view?** `OpenEntityManagerInViewInterceptor` keeps the `EntityManager` open for the whole web request (default `spring.jpa.open-in-view=true`, with a warning at start-up). It allows lazy loading in controllers and serialisation, and holds a database connection for the entire request.
8. `MultipleBagFetchException`**?** Fetching two `List` collections (bags) in one query is rejected because of the Cartesian product. Use `Set`, fetch one collection per query, or batch fetching.
9. **Why is paging with a collection fetch dangerous?** Hibernate cannot apply `LIMIT` to a joined collection and paginates in memory (warning HHH000104). Page the root ids first, then fetch the associations for those ids.
10. **How is optimistic locking implemented?** A `@Version` attribute is included in the `UPDATE ... WHERE id = ?` `AND version = ?`; zero updated rows raises `ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException`.
11. `IDENTITY` **or** `SEQUENCE` **id generation?** `IDENTITY` forces an immediate insert to obtain the key, which disables JDBC insert batching. `SEQUENCE` with an allocation size permits batching.
12. **What must** `equals` **and** `hashCode` **of an entity respect?** They must be stable across the entity lifecycle: use a business key or a database-independent identifier assigned at construction; an id generated at persist time changes `hashCode` of an object already stored in a `HashSet`.
13. `save` **in** `CrudRepository`**: persist or merge?** `SimpleJpaRepository.save` calls `persist` for a new entity (`isNew`, determined by a null id or version) and `merge` otherwise; `merge` issues a `SELECT` first and copies state onto a managed instance.
14. **What is a derived query versus** `@Query`**?** Derived queries are parsed from the method name (`findByStatusAndCreatedAtAfter`); `@Query` takes JPQL or native SQL and is clearer for anything beyond two predicates.

### Transactions

1. **What does** `@Transactional` **do?** A proxy with `TransactionInterceptor` obtains a `PlatformTransactionManager`, begins a transaction according to the propagation, invokes the method, commits, or rolls back on a `RuntimeException` or `Error`.
2. **Which exceptions roll back by default?** Unchecked exceptions and errors. Checked exceptions commit unless `rollbackFor` is specified.
3. **Explain the propagation types.** `REQUIRED` (join or create, default), `REQUIRES_NEW` (suspend and start independent), `NESTED` (savepoint), `SUPPORTS`, `NOT_SUPPORTED`, `MANDATORY`, `NEVER`.
4. **What does** `readOnly = true` **do?** It is a hint: Hibernate skips dirty checking (flush mode `MANUAL`) and some drivers or routing data sources choose a read replica. It does not prevent writes at database level on its own.
5. **What are the isolation levels and anomalies?** `READ_UNCOMMITTED`, `READ_COMMITTED` (PostgreSQL default), `REPEATABLE_READ`, `SERIALIZABLE`. They prevent, progressively, dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantoms; PostgreSQL implements snapshot isolation at `REPEATABLE_READ` and may abort with a serialisation failure that must be retried.
6. **How is a lost update prevented?** Optimistic locking with `@Version`, pessimistic locking (`SELECT ... FOR` `UPDATE`, `LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE`), or an atomic update statement.
7. **Why does a long transaction exhaust the Hikari pool?** The connection is held from the first statement to commit; a transaction that waits on an HTTP call keeps the connection idle-in-transaction. Keep remote calls outside transactions.
8. **How is work run after a successful commit?** `@TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT)` or `TransactionSynchronizationManager.registerSynchronization`.
9. **How should deadlocks be handled?** Acquire locks in a consistent order, keep transactions short, and retry the transaction on `CannotAcquireLockException` or `DeadlockLoserDataAccessException`.
10. **What is** `TransactionTemplate` **for?** Programmatic transaction boundaries inside a method, where a declarative annotation does not fit (self-invocation, several transactions in one flow).

### Security, JWT and OAuth 2.0

1. **How does Spring Security plug into the servlet stack?** `DelegatingFilterProxy` (registered by Boot under the bean name `springSecurityFilterChain`) delegates to `FilterChainProxy`, which selects the first matching `SecurityFilterChain` and runs its ordered filters.
2. **What is** `SecurityContextHolder`**?** A holder, thread-local by default, of the `SecurityContext` that contains the `Authentication` of the current request; it is cleared at the end of each request.
3. **How does authentication proceed?** A filter creates an unauthenticated `Authentication`; `AuthenticationManager` (`ProviderManager`) asks `AuthenticationProvider`s, for instance `DaoAuthenticationProvider` with a `UserDetailsService` and `PasswordEncoder`; the result is stored in the context.
4. **401 versus 403?** 401 means the request is not authenticated (or the credentials are invalid) and is produced by the `AuthenticationEntryPoint`. 403 means the authenticated principal lacks permission and is produced by the `AccessDeniedHandler`.
5. `hasRole("ADMIN")` **versus** `hasAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN")`**?** They are equivalent: `hasRole` adds the `ROLE_` prefix. Mismatches arise when the stored authorities lack the prefix.
6. **Why** `BCrypt`**/**`Argon2` **and not** `SHA-256` **for passwords?** Password hashing must be slow and salted so that brute force is expensive; fast hashes are cheap to attack on GPUs. `DelegatingPasswordEncoder` stores an `{id}` prefix and allows migration of algorithms.
7. **When is CSRF protection needed?** When authentication is carried automatically by the browser (session cookies). A stateless API with an `Authorization` header token is not exposed in the same way, and CSRF can be disabled for it.
8. **Session or token authentication?** Sessions are stateful and revocable, and need shared storage (Spring Session with Redis) when scaled. Tokens are stateless and scale easily, but are hard to revoke before expiry.
9. **Structure of a JWT?** `base64url(header).base64url(payload).base64url(signature)`. HS256 signs with a shared secret (HMAC), RS256 and ES256 with a private key and verify with a public key.
10. **What must a JWT verifier check?** Signature with the expected algorithm (never trust the `alg` header: `none` and algorithm confusion attacks), `exp`, `nbf`, `iss`, `aud`, and a small clock skew allowance.
11. **How are refresh tokens secured?** Long-lived, stored hashed server-side, rotated on every use with reuse detection (reuse of an old token revokes the family), delivered in an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite` cookie.
12. **Where should the access token live in a browser?** An `HttpOnly` cookie is not readable by scripts (XSS cannot steal it, but CSRF must be handled); `localStorage` is readable by any script on the page.
13. **Explain the authorisation code flow with PKCE.** The client sends the user to the authorisation server with a `code_challenge`; after login it receives a code at the redirect URI and exchanges it together with the `code_verifier` for tokens. PKCE binds the code to the client instance and protects public clients.
14. **Resource server versus client?** A resource server validates access tokens and serves an API (`oauth2ResourceServer().jwt()`); a client obtains tokens on behalf of a user (`oauth2Login`, `oauth2Client`).
15. **Why does** `@PreAuthorize` **not apply?** `@EnableMethodSecurity` is missing, or the call is a self-invocation, or the class is not a proxied bean.

### Microservices and resilience

1. **When should a system not be split into microservices?** When the team is small, the domain boundaries are unclear, or operational maturity (CI/CD, observability, on-call) is missing. A modular monolith keeps boundaries without network failure modes.
2. **Why database per service?** Services own their data to deploy and evolve independently; sharing a schema couples them through the database. Cross-service consistency then needs sagas and events instead of joins and transactions.
3. **What is a saga?** A sequence of local transactions where each step publishes an event or command, and failures trigger compensating transactions. Choreography has services react to events; orchestration has a coordinator drive the steps.
4. **Why not two-phase commit?** It blocks resources while the coordinator decides, reduces availability, and is not supported across heterogeneous systems such as a database and Kafka.
5. **Explain the circuit breaker states.** Closed (calls pass, failures counted), open (calls fail fast for a wait duration), half-open (a limited number of trial calls decide whether to close or reopen). Resilience4j's `CircuitBreaker` opens when the failure rate exceeds a threshold over a sliding window.
6. **Why must retries use backoff and jitter?** Immediate retries multiply the load on a struggling dependency (a retry storm). Exponential backoff spaces attempts and jitter prevents synchronised retry waves.
7. **When is a retry safe?** When the operation is idempotent or carries an idempotency key, and the error is transient. A non-idempotent `POST` retried without a key can duplicate side effects.
8. **What is a bulkhead?** Isolation of resource pools (threads or semaphore permits) per dependency, so that one slow dependency cannot consume all capacity.
9. **What is the order of Resilience4j decorators?** By default, from outside to inside: `Retry`, `CircuitBreaker`, `RateLimiter`, `TimeLimiter`, `Bulkhead` (as aspect order `Retry ( CircuitBreaker ( RateLimiter ( TimeLimiter (` `Bulkhead ( Function ) ) ) ) )`); each can be reordered through aspect order properties.
10. **What does an API gateway do?** Single entry point: routing, authentication, rate limiting, TLS termination, request and response transformation, aggregated cross-cutting concerns. Spring Cloud Gateway is reactive, based on routes, predicates and filters.
11. **Client-side versus server-side load balancing?** The client holds the instance list and chooses (Spring Cloud LoadBalancer); a server-side balancer (Kubernetes Service, a cloud load balancer) chooses for the client. In Kubernetes the Service DNS name is usually sufficient.
12. **How is a trace followed across services?** A trace id and span id are propagated in the W3C `traceparent` header; Micrometer Tracing adds them to the MDC for log correlation and exports spans to a backend. `@Async` and thread pools need context propagation.
13. **What is the transactional outbox and when is it used?** An outbox table written in the business transaction and relayed to the broker; it solves the dual-write problem with at-least-once delivery.
14. **What is CQRS?** Separate models for commands (writes) and queries (reads), possibly with separate stores updated from events; it adds eventual consistency and complexity and fits read-heavy or complex-reporting cases only.

### Kafka, messaging and caching

1. **Queue versus log?** A queue deletes messages after acknowledgement and tracks delivery per message; a log retains records, and consumers track offsets, which allows replay and multiple groups.
2. **How is parallelism achieved in Kafka?** By partitions: each partition is consumed by one member of a group, so the number of partitions bounds consumer parallelism.
3. **Why can messages be processed twice, and what is the remedy?** Offset commit and processing are separate steps. Idempotent consumers (unique event id, upsert) make duplicates harmless.
4. **What guarantees does** `acks=all` **give?** The leader acknowledges after all in-sync replicas have the record; with `min.insync.replicas=2` and replication factor 3, an acknowledged write survives the loss of one broker.
5. **What is a rebalance and why is it costly?** Reassignment of partitions after membership change; with the eager protocol all consumers stop. Cooperative assignors, static membership and tuned timeouts reduce the impact.
6. **How does** `DefaultErrorHandler` **retry?** It seeks back to the failed offset and redelivers according to a `BackOff` (default ten attempts without delay), then calls a recoverer such as `DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer`.
7. **When are retry topics preferable to blocking retries?** When failures are transient, order is not required, and stalling a partition is unacceptable; the price is lost ordering and more topics.
8. **What does Kafka exactly-once cover?** Idempotent producer plus transactions with offsets committed in the transaction (consume-transform-produce within Kafka). External effects need idempotence.
9. **RabbitMQ: what are exchanges for?** Routing: producers publish to exchanges, which distribute messages to queues by binding rules (`direct`, `topic`, `fanout`, `headers`).
10. **Why is** `@Scheduled` **unsafe in a cluster?** Every instance runs it. Use ShedLock, a Kubernetes `CronJob`, or Quartz with a clustered JDBC store.
11. **What is a cache stampede?** Many concurrent misses of one expired key reaching the backend. Single flight (`sync = true`), TTL jitter and background refresh mitigate it.
12. **How is cache consistency kept with the database?** Evict after commit, use TTLs as a safety net, route all writes through one component, and accept bounded staleness explicitly.

### Testing, Actuator and performance

1. **Test pyramid in a Spring project?** Many fast unit tests without a context, fewer slice tests (`@WebMvcTest`, `@DataJpaTest`), few full `@SpringBootTest` integration tests with real infrastructure through Testcontainers.
2. `@WebMvcTest` **versus** `@SpringBootTest`**?** `@WebMvcTest` loads only MVC infrastructure and the named controllers, with collaborators replaced by `@MockitoBean` (Boot 3.4; `@MockBean` before). `@SpringBootTest` loads the full context.
3. **Why are Spring tests slow?** Each distinct configuration (different mocks, properties, `@DirtiesContext`) creates a new application context that the test context cache cannot share. Standardise the configuration and avoid `@DirtiesContext`.
4. **Why Testcontainers instead of H2?** H2 differs in SQL dialect, locking, types and isolation, so tests pass on H2 and fail on PostgreSQL. Testcontainers runs the real database; `@ServiceConnection` wires its properties automatically.
5. **What are Actuator health groups?** Named subsets of health indicators, including `liveness` and `readiness` used by Kubernetes probes; groups are configured under `management.endpoint.health.group.*`.
6. **How are Actuator endpoints secured?** Expose only the required endpoints (`management.endpoints.web.exposure.include`), put them on a separate management port or behind security rules, and never expose `env`, `heapdump` or `threaddump` publicly.
7. **What is metric cardinality and why does it matter?** The number of distinct tag combinations. A tag with unbounded values (user id, URL with path variables) creates a time series per value and exhausts the monitoring system.
8. **RED and USE methods?** RED (rate, errors, duration) for services; USE (utilisation, saturation, errors) for resources such as thread pools and connection pools.
9. **How is a slow endpoint investigated?** Check metrics (`http.server.requests` percentiles), traces to locate the slow span, thread dumps (`jcmd <pid> Thread.print`) for blocking, a JFR or async-profiler recording for CPU, and SQL logs for the database.
10. **How does Hikari pool sizing work?** A small pool (often `cores * 2 + effective spindles` as a starting point) with a queue is faster than a large one; `maximumPoolSize` and `connectionTimeout` are tuned against database capacity and transaction length.
11. **Platform threads versus virtual threads for MVC?** Virtual threads (JDK 21, `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true`) remove the thread-per-request limit for blocking I/O; CPU-bound work, pinned `synchronized` sections and limited downstream pools remain constraints.
12. **How is start-up time reduced?** Lazy initialisation, fewer auto-configurations and classpath scanning, Class Data Sharing or the AOT cache, and GraalVM native image for the extreme case at the cost of build time and reflection configuration.

### Docker, Kubernetes and CI/CD

1. **What is a layered jar?** An executable jar with a `layers.idx` that groups files into dependency and application layers, extracted into separate Docker layers for cache efficiency.
2. **How is memory sized for a JVM in a container?** `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` for the heap, with headroom for metaspace, thread stacks, direct memory and native memory; exceeding the container limit is `OOMKilled` (exit code 137).
3. **How does graceful shutdown work end to end?** Endpoint removal and a `preStop` sleep, `SIGTERM`, readiness down, `server.shutdown=graceful` drains active requests within the timeout, the context closes, and the grace period must exceed all of it.
4. **Liveness versus readiness?** Liveness restarts a broken container; readiness controls traffic. External dependencies belong in readiness at most.
5. **What gates a rolling update?** The readiness probe, together with `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable`.
6. **How does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler work?** It scales replicas to keep an average metric (CPU utilisation relative to requests, or custom metrics) at the target, between minimum and maximum.
7. **ConfigMap versus Secret?** Both inject configuration; Secrets are for sensitive values, base64-encoded in the API and protected by RBAC and optional encryption at rest.
8. **How are environment variables mapped to Spring properties?** By relaxed binding: `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` maps to `spring.datasource.url`.
9. **What does a CI pipeline for a Spring Boot service contain?** Checkout, JDK setup with dependency cache, `mvn` `verify` (unit and Testcontainers integration tests), static and dependency scanning, image build and push with an immutable tag, deployment to staging, approval, production.
10. **Surefire versus Failsafe?** Unit tests in `test` versus integration tests in `integration-test` with verification in `verify`.
11. **Blue-green versus canary versus rolling?** Full environment switch with instant rollback; progressive traffic shift with metric analysis; gradual pod replacement in place.
12. **What does a secret leak response consist of?** Revoke and rotate immediately, assess usage in audit logs, remove the secret from the repository and history, and add preventive scanning.
13. **How are database migrations kept compatible with rolling updates?** Expand-and-contract: additive changes first, code migration second, removal in a later release.
14. **How are Docker Compose and Testcontainers used by Spring Boot?** `spring-boot-docker-compose` starts the compose services for development and derives connection details; Testcontainers with `@ServiceConnection` does the same for tests.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Strong answers start from the mechanism: the real class, the order of steps, and the property that controls it.

- Group questions by failure mode: proxy bypass, lazy loading, transaction boundaries, token verification, retries and idempotency are asked in many forms.
- Every answer should end with the trade-off or the pitfall, which is what distinguishes experience from recitation.
- Practise answering aloud against the clock: two minutes for the mechanism, one minute for the pitfall.

sections.title: System Design Scenarios for Spring Services

blocks.text:
A system design interview for a Java role asks for a service that works, with numbers, a data model, an API, failure handling and the Spring components that implement it. The method is the same for each scenario: state functional and non-functional requirements, estimate load, define the API and the data model, draw the components, then examine bottlenecks and failure modes. The three scenarios below use the techniques of the whole guide: caching, idempotency, the outbox, rate limiting and resilience. Estimates are order-of-magnitude assumptions, stated as such, and not measurements.

### Scenario 1: a URL shortener

**Requirements.** Create a short code for a long URL (`POST /urls`), redirect from `GET /{code}`. Redirects must be fast (p99 under 20 ms) and highly available; creation may be slower. Codes are unique; optional custom aliases and expiry.

**Estimates (assumed).** 100 million new URLs per year, a read to write ratio of 100:1, so about 10 billion redirects per year, an average of 320 per second and a peak of about 10 000 per second. A record of code, long URL and metadata takes about 500 bytes, which gives roughly 50 GB per year.

**Code generation.** A 7-character code over a 62-symbol alphabet (digits, upper and lower case letters) gives 62^7 = 3 521 614 606 208 codes, enough for 35 000 years at the assumed rate. The code is the base-62 encoding of a unique number. The following program shows the encoding and decoding, run on the build machine.

blocks.title: Base62.java

blocks.code:
$ java Base62.java
id=1                code=1        decoded=1
id=61               code=z        decoded=61
id=62               code=10       decoded=62
id=125              code=21       decoded=125
id=1000000          code=4C92     decoded=1000000
id=3521614606207    code=zzzzzzz  decoded=3521614606207
62^7 = 3521614606208 codes of length 7
blocks.title: Output of the base-62 encoder (run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
A database sequence that is incremented per URL yields unique numbers without coordination, but sequential codes are guessable, which leaks the creation rate and allows enumeration. Remedies: apply a bijective scrambling of the number (a multiplication modulo a prime near 62^7, or a block cipher on the id), or draw ids from a generator that mixes time and random bits, with a unique index as the final arbiter and a retry on conflict. A hash of the URL (truncated) is not unique and needs collision handling.

**Components.**

blocks.text:
**Data model.** One table `short_url(code varchar(10) primary key, long_url text not null, created_at` `timestamptz, expires_at timestamptz, owner_id bigint)`. The primary key lookup is the only hot query, so a relational database suffices at this scale; sharding by `code` hash becomes relevant above a few terabytes or write rates the primary cannot absorb.

**Redirect path.** `GET /{code}` is cache-aside: Redis lookup, on a miss a primary-key read and a write-back with a TTL of 24 hours. The response is `302 Found` with `Location` when click analytics matter (a `301` is cached by browsers and hides later requests from the service). Unknown codes are cached negatively for a short time to protect the database from scans.

blocks.title: RedirectController.java

blocks.text:
The regular expression in the mapping rejects malformed codes before any lookup. `UrlService.resolve` is annotated `@Cacheable(cacheNames = "urls", sync = true)` and returns an `Optional<String>` (Spring caches the unwrapped value and handles `Optional` specially, so a missing value is not stored unless null caching is enabled).

**Bottlenecks and failure modes.** A viral link is one hot key: the cache absorbs it, and a local in-process cache (Caffeine, a few seconds) in front of Redis removes the network hop. Redis loss means a cold start with a stampede on the database: single flight and a connection-pool limit protect it. Analytics (click counts) must not be a synchronous database write per redirect; the service publishes a click event to Kafka or increments a Redis counter and aggregates asynchronously. Expired links are removed by a scheduled job that is made cluster-safe (see the scheduling chapter).

### Scenario 2: an order service

**Requirements.** Customers place orders for several items; payment and stock reservation must both succeed or the order is cancelled; no double charge when a client retries; order status is visible; peak 500 orders per second during sales.

**Decomposition.** `order-service` (owns orders), `payment-service`, `inventory-service` and `notification-service`, each with its own database. Communication for the order flow is event-driven with a saga.

blocks.text: **API and idempotency.** `POST /orders` requires an `Idempotency-Key` header chosen by the client (a UUID). The service stores the key with the order under a unique constraint on `(customer_id, idempotency_key)`. A retry with the same key returns the original response instead of creating a second order. This turns client and gateway retries, which are inevitable, into a safe operation.

blocks.title: OrderStatus.java

blocks.text:
The transition table is what makes event handling safe against reordering and duplicates: an event that asks for an illegal transition (`PaymentFailed` after `CONFIRMED`) is ignored or routed to review. The aggregate carries a `@Version` field so that two events processed concurrently cannot both succeed.

**Saga.** `OrderCreated` is published through the outbox. `inventory-service` reserves stock and emits `StockReserved` or `StockRejected`; `payment-service` authorises payment on `StockReserved` and emits `PaymentCaptured` or `PaymentFailed`. The order service moves to `CONFIRMED` on `PaymentCaptured`. On `PaymentFailed` it moves to `CANCELLED` and publishes `OrderCancelled`, which makes inventory release the reservation (the compensation). Every consumer is idempotent by event id. This is choreography; with more steps an orchestrator (a state machine in `order-service`) is easier to reason about and to monitor.

**Resilience.** The gateway applies a timeout and a rate limit. Calls to the payment provider (the one synchronous dependency) use a timeout, a circuit breaker and a bounded retry with backoff and an idempotency key at the provider. A stuck saga (no event after five minutes) is detected by a scheduled query and escalated or compensated.

**Reads.** `GET /orders/{id}` is answered by `order-service` from its own database. A customer-facing view that joins order, payment and shipment data is built from events into a read model, so that no request fans out to three services.

**Bottlenecks.** At 500 orders per second the order table insert rate is modest; the limiting factors are the payment provider, Kafka partitioning (key by `orderId` for per-order ordering, enough partitions for consumer parallelism) and database connection pools. Outbox polling is replaced by change data capture if latency or load matters.

### Scenario 3: a rate-limited public API

**Requirements.** Limit each API key to 10 requests per second with a burst of 20; reject excess with `429 Too Many` `Requests`; the limit must hold across all instances; the limiter must not become a single point of failure; limits differ by plan.

**Algorithms.** Fixed window counters are simple but allow double the rate at window boundaries. Sliding windows are accurate and cost more state. The token bucket permits bursts up to its capacity and refills at a constant rate, which matches API semantics: capacity 20, refill 10 tokens per second. In a distributed setting the bucket state (tokens and last refill time) lives in Redis and is updated atomically by a Lua script, since a read-modify-write from several instances would race.

blocks.text: Spring Cloud Gateway implements this with the `RequestRateLimiter` filter and `RedisRateLimiter`:

blocks.code:
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      host: redis
      timeout: 200ms
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: public-api
          uri: lb://order-service
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/**
          filters:
            - name: RequestRateLimiter
              args:
                redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 10
                redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 20
                redis-rate-limiter.requestedTokens: 1
                key-resolver: "#{@apiKeyResolver}"
                deny-empty-key: true
                empty-key-status-code: 401
blocks.title: application.yml (gateway)
RateLimitConfig.java

blocks.text:
What to notice: the key resolver decides what is limited (here the API key; an unauthenticated route would use the client address, which is unreliable behind proxies unless `X-Forwarded-For` is configured and trusted); `RedisRateLimiter` rejects with status 429 and adds `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `X-RateLimit-Burst-Capacity`, `X-RateLimit-Replenish-Rate` and `X-RateLimit-Requested-Tokens` headers; and per-plan limits require a custom `RateLimiter` bean or one route per plan, because the `RedisRateLimiter` configuration is per route.

**Failure behaviour.** When Redis is unreachable the Spring Cloud Gateway Redis limiter logs and allows the request (fail open), which favours availability; abuse-sensitive routes may need fail-closed behaviour through a custom limiter. Clients are expected to honour `Retry-After` and use exponential backoff with jitter; otherwise rejected requests are retried immediately and the limiter amplifies the load it is protecting against.

**Layers.** The edge (CDN, load balancer) applies coarse per-IP limits against volumetric abuse; the gateway applies per-key quotas; the services use bulkheads for protection of their own resources. Each layer protects a different resource.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How would the design change by a factor of ten in load? State the first component that saturates and the lever for it: stateless instances scale horizontally behind the load balancer; the cache absorbs reads, with replicas or local caches for hot keys; the database needs read replicas, then partitioning by a key chosen from the access pattern; Kafka needs more partitions and consumers; synchronous dependencies need bulkheads and degradation. Name the metric that shows saturation for each (CPU, pool wait time, cache hit ratio, consumer lag).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
A design answer states requirements, estimates, API, data model, components and then bottlenecks and failure modes, in that order.

- Unique ids come from a sequence encoded in base 62; the code space is sized from the creation rate.
- Idempotency keys, a state machine with versioned aggregates and idempotent consumers make order flows safe under retries and reordering.
- A distributed token bucket needs atomic state in Redis; the failure policy (open or closed) is an explicit decision.

    name: orders
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 25s
  threads:
    virtual:
      enabled: false              # true on JDK 21+ (Boot 3.2+) for virtual threads
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orders
    username: orders
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 10
      connection-timeout: 3000
      max-lifetime: 1500000
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate
    properties:
      hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size: 32
      hibernate.jdbc.batch_size: 50
  flyway:
    enabled: true
  jackson:
    default-property-inclusion: non_null
  mvc:
    problemdetails:
      enabled: true
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,metrics,prometheus
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true
      show-details: when-authorized
logging:
  level:
    root: INFO
    com.example: DEBUG

blocks.text:
**Method for each study session.** Read the concept section with the diagram, close the guide and redraw the diagram from memory, then run the worked example and change one thing to break it (remove a timeout, add a self-invocation, disable a unique constraint) and observe the failure named in the problems section. A mechanism that has been broken deliberately is remembered better than one that has only been read.

**Interview rehearsal.** From week 3 onward, answer five random questions from the bank every day with a timer, aloud. Record the answer, and check that it contains a class or property name, the order of steps, and a pitfall. For the design scenarios, use the template: requirements, estimates, API, data model, diagram, bottlenecks, failure modes.

**Portfolio.** The final project demonstrates the guide better than any answer: a multi-service application with CI, containers, tests with Testcontainers, security with JWT, a Kafka flow with an outbox, and a README that documents the decisions and the measured behaviour. A hiring engineer reads the repository for tests, commit history and the handling of failure cases before reading the code in detail.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
The cheat sheets are indexes into the guide, not substitutes for it; a row is useful only when the mechanism behind it is understood.

- Study in the order container, data, security, distribution, quality, delivery; later topics depend on proxies and transactions.
- Break every worked example once; the failure modes are the interview material.
- Rehearse aloud with a timer; structure beats volume.

sections.title: Putting it Together: One Request through a Spring Boot Microservice

blocks.text:
### Microservice

Every chapter of this guide describes one mechanism in isolation. A production request passes through all of them in a few milliseconds, and a defect at any point appears to the user as the same symptom: a slow or failed response. This chapter follows a single `POST /api/orders` from the client to the consumer that reacts to the resulting event, naming at each step the component involved, the Spring class that implements it, the failure that can occur there, and the place to look when it does. It is the integration exercise for the whole guide and also the structure of a strong answer to the interview question "what happens when a request arrives at your service?".

### Concept and mechanism

The scenario: a client submits an order with a bearer token. The request is rate limited and authenticated at the gateway, routed to `order-service`, processed through the servlet filter chain and `DispatcherServlet`, validated, executed in a database transaction that writes the order and an outbox row, and answered with `201 Created`. Afterwards the outbox relay publishes `OrderCreated` to Kafka, a consumer in another service processes it idempotently and evicts a cache entry. Metrics and a trace cover the whole path.

### Worked example

The controller and service of `order-service` show steps 5 to 9 in code. The entity and repository follow the earlier chapters; the outbox classes are those of the Kafka chapter.

blocks.title: OrderController.java
CreateOrderRequest.java
OrderPlacementService.java

blocks.text:
What to notice: the idempotency check and the insert are in one transaction, and a unique constraint on `(customer_id, idempotency_key)` closes the race between two concurrent retries (the loser receives `DataIntegrityViolationException` and the controller advice maps it to a lookup of the existing order); `create` is a private method called within the transactional `place`, which is correct because the transaction is already open; the unchecked `IllegalStateException` rolls back the order and the outbox row together; and the counter is a Micrometer meter without unbounded tags.

### Hands-on

A trace of the request in the logs of the two services, with the trace id carried by Micrometer Tracing in the MDC (logging pattern `%5p [${spring.application.name},%X{traceId},%X{spanId}]`). The lines are the typical form and were not produced on the build machine.

blocks.text:
The same trace id appears in the gateway, in the service, in the relay (the span of the scheduled run links to the stored trace context when the outbox row keeps the `traceparent`) and in the consumer, because Micrometer Tracing propagates the W3C `traceparent` in HTTP and Kafka headers when observation of the Kafka template and listener containers is enabled (`spring.kafka.template.observation-enabled` and `spring.kafka.listener.observation-enabled` in Boot 3.2 and later). A scheduled relay has no incoming request, so it must store the trace context in the outbox row to continue the trace, or it starts a new trace and the link is lost.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: the order endpoint is slow and the cause is unknown

**Scenario.** The 99th percentile of `POST /api/orders` rises from 80 ms to 1.8 s after a release; no errors are reported. **Symptoms.** Dashboards show higher `http.server.requests` percentiles; CPU is normal. **Diagnosis.** Follow the path. Open a slow trace and read the span durations: gateway, controller, database. If the database span dominates, check `hikaricp.connections.pending` and `hikaricp.connections.acquire`; if acquisition is slow, the pool is saturated, and `pg_stat_activity` shows connections `idle in transaction`. If the handler span dominates without database time, take two thread dumps ten seconds apart (`jcmd <pid> Thread.print`) and compare the stacks of the worker threads. Enable `spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true` temporarily to count statements per request. **Root cause.** The release added a synchronous call to a tax service inside the `@Transactional` method; each request held a connection for the duration of that call, and the pool of 10 connections became the limit. **Fix.** Move the call before the transaction or make the data available through the event flow; add timeouts to the client; keep the transaction to the two inserts. **Prevention.** Load test with realistic dependencies; alert on pool wait time, not only on pool usage.

#### Problem 2: the order exists but no downstream service reacted

**Scenario.** Support reports orders that never reach payment. **Symptoms.** Rows in `orders` without a matching payment; no errors in `order-service`. **Diagnosis.** Check the outbox: `SELECT count(*), min(created_at) FROM` `outbox_event WHERE sent_at IS NULL`. A growing count and an old minimum mean the relay is not publishing: look at the relay logs for `TimeoutException` from the Kafka send, check `@EnableScheduling`, and check whether the relay transaction is blocked by a long-held lock. If the outbox is empty, check consumer lag and the dead-letter topic of the payment service. **Root cause.** The relay method threw on a record larger than `max.request.size`; the transaction rolled back and the same record was retried at the head of the batch every 500 ms, blocking all later records. **Fix.** Handle per-record failures (catch, mark the row as failed with an attempt counter, continue), and publish oversized payloads by reference. **Prevention.** Alert on the age of the oldest unsent outbox row and on the dead-letter topic rate.

### Questions to expect

1. **What happens when a request reaches a Spring Boot application?** The connector hands it to a worker thread; the filter chain runs (including the security filters); `DispatcherServlet` finds the handler, resolves arguments, validates, invokes the controller, converts the result; interceptors and exception resolvers wrap the process; the response is written and the thread returns to the pool.
2. **Where are transactions started in that flow, and why not in the controller?** At the service boundary through the proxy; a transaction in the controller would include serialisation and filter time, hold a connection longer and mix web and persistence concerns.
3. **How are duplicate orders from client retries prevented?** An idempotency key stored under a unique constraint, with the original response returned on repetition.
4. **How is the event published without losing it?** Through the transactional outbox, relayed to Kafka with at-least-once delivery.
5. **How is one request traced across services?** Propagation of the `traceparent` header through HTTP and Kafka, correlation in the MDC, and a trace backend; asynchronous hand-offs need context propagation.
6. **What is checked first when latency rises?** Percentiles by endpoint, then traces to locate the slow span, then pool and thread metrics, then thread dumps and SQL statistics.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
A request is a chain of mechanisms; naming them in order, with the class and the failure at each step, is the strongest demonstration of understanding.

- The synchronous path ends at the database commit; everything after it is asynchronous and at-least-once.
- Idempotency keys, the outbox and idempotent consumers make retries and duplicates harmless at each hop.
- Metrics locate the symptom, traces locate the step, thread dumps and SQL logs locate the cause.
